In a broader, somewhat literary or formal sense, animus can also refer to the central spirit, intention, or driving force behind something — not necessarily hostile, but the motivating essence of something.

"The animus of the entire movement was a desire for justice."

Here, animus means the soul or driving spirit of something. This usage is less common in everyday conversation but appears in more elevated writing and academic discourse. You can think of it as the animating force — the life or purpose that breathes energy into a cause, work, or effort.

SituationWhat "animus" means
Everyday languageStrong, targeted hostility or deep-seated prejudice toward someone or something
Legal languageThe intention or motive behind an action, especially a biased or malicious one
Jungian psychologyThe unconscious masculine side of a woman's psyche
Formal/literaryThe driving spirit, motivation, or animating force behind something

If you remember nothing else: animus is the deep, underlying hostility or prejudice someone holds toward a specific person or group. It's not casual dislike. It's the kind of animosity that motivates behavior — often unfair, discriminatory, or aggressive behavior. When someone acts with animus, there's a personal, charged, targeted ill will behind it.

That one core meaning will serve you correctly in the vast majority of situations where you encounter this word.
770: The ankh is an ancient Egyptian symbol that looks like a cross, except that instead of having a plain top arm, it has an oval loop (like a teardrop or a handle) sitting on top of it. Picture the letter T, and then replace the top with an oval — that's the ankh. It is one of the most recognizable symbols ever created by any civilization.

The single most important thing to know is this: the ankh means "life."

Not just everyday, ordinary life — but life in its fullest, most powerful sense. It stands for the life force itself, the energy that animates living beings. In ancient Egypt, it also meant eternal life and immortality — the idea that life does not end with physical death, but continues forever in another form.

Think of it as the ancient Egyptian answer to the question: what is the essence of being alive? Their answer was the ankh.
Where it comes from and who used it

The ankh belongs to ancient Egyptian civilization, which flourished for over 3,000 years along the Nile River in northeastern Africa. It is one of the oldest symbols in human history, appearing in Egyptian art and writing as far back as the Early Dynastic Period (around 3100 BCE).

In the ancient Egyptian writing system (hieroglyphics), the ankh was also a hieroglyph — a picture-character that literally meant "life" or "to live." So it wasn't just a symbol people drew; it was also a word they wrote.
How it appeared in Egyptian religion and art

The ankh was deeply tied to gods, pharaohs (kings), and the afterlife.

Gods holding the ankh: In Egyptian religious art, gods are almost always shown carrying an ankh — usually gripped by its loop, like a key held in the hand. This was extremely meaningful. When a god held the ankh, it meant they possessed and controlled the power of life. The god Osiris (ruler of the afterlife), the goddess Isis (goddess of magic and healing), Ra (the sun god), and Anubis (god of death and embalming) are all commonly shown with the ankh. Essentially, nearly every major Egyptian deity was associated with it.

The "breath of life" gesture: In many paintings and carvings, a god is shown holding the ankh up to the nose or lips of the pharaoh. This gesture symbolized the god breathing eternal life directly into the king. It was the highest blessing imaginable — the divine gift of living forever.

Pharaohs and the ankh: Pharaohs were considered to be living gods on Earth, and they were frequently depicted holding the ankh themselves, to show that they too carried the life force. It was a statement of their divine power and immortality.
How it was used as an object

The ankh wasn't only a picture or a word — it was also made into physical objects that people actually used.

Amulets: Ordinary Egyptians wore small ankh amulets (charms) made of faience (a type of glazed ceramic), gold, or other materials. They wore these around their necks or kept them close to their bodies, believing the symbol would protect them and attract the life force to them. Essentially, wearing an ankh was a way of saying I want to live well and live long.

Mirrors: Interestingly, many ancient Egyptian hand mirrors were made in the shape of the ankh — the oval loop at the top was the mirror glass itself, and the cross below was the handle. Some scholars believe this was deliberate: a mirror shows you your own living face, which is itself a reflection of life.

Tomb objects: Ankh symbols and amulets were placed inside tombs with the dead. This was not merely decorative — it was a practical spiritual measure. Egyptians believed in a rich, detailed afterlife, and placing an ankh with the deceased was meant to help protect them, ensure their eternal life, and assist them in the journey beyond death.

While life is its primary meaning, the ankh carried deeper layers of meaning within Egyptian thought:

Union and wholeness: Some Egyptologists believe the ankh symbolized the union of opposites — male and female, the earthly and the divine, the mortal and the immortal. The loop at the top and the cross below were sometimes interpreted as two complementary forces coming together to create life.

The sun and the horizon: A few scholars have connected the ankh's shape to the image of the sun rising above the horizon, with the oval representing the sun and the cross representing rays of light or the horizon line. Since the sun was the supreme source of life in Egyptian thinking (and was worshipped as the god Ra), this connection made the ankh even more charged with meaning.

The key to the afterlife: Because it appeared so prominently in funeral contexts, the ankh was sometimes called the "key of life" or the "key to the Nile." It was thought to literally unlock the gates of the afterlife, allowing the soul to pass into eternity. This is why in many tomb paintings, the ankh appears in the hands of gods who guide the dead through the underworld.
The ankh in the modern world

The ankh did not stay locked in ancient history. Today, it appears in many different contexts:

As jewelry and fashion: The ankh is one of the most popular symbols used in jewelry worldwide. People wear it as necklaces, bracelets, and earrings — often simply because they find it beautiful or meaningful as a general symbol of life.

In African identity movements: The ankh has been reclaimed by many people of African descent as a symbol of African heritage, pride, and spiritual roots. Because ancient Egypt was an African civilization, the ankh connects people to that history and identity.

In alternative spirituality: The ankh is used by various modern spiritual groups, including Wiccans and other neo-pagan traditions, as a symbol of life, rebirth, and the divine feminine.

In popular culture: The ankh appears in movies, video games, books, and artwork as a shorthand for ancient Egypt, immortality, or mystical power.
The single sentence that captures it all

If you had to reduce the ankh to one sentence, it would be this:

The ankh is an ancient Egyptian cross-with-a-loop symbol that represents life, eternal life, and the divine power to give or sustain life — used by gods, pharaohs, and ordinary people alike for thousands of years.

Every time you see it — whether in a museum painting of a god, or on a piece of modern jewelry — you are looking at humanity's oldest and most iconic answer to one of life's deepest questions: what does it mean to truly live?
771: "Annals" is a noun that refers to the formal, written historical record of events — essentially, documented history. It is almost always used in its plural form. You will rarely, if ever, see the singular "annal" in everyday writing or speech.
Two senses, from narrow to broad

The original, precise sense is a year-by-year written record of events. Imagine historians or monks in ancient and medieval times sitting down at the end of each year and carefully writing down everything significant that had happened — wars, the deaths of kings, floods, discoveries. Each year's entry was one "annal." Together, all those entries formed the "annals." The Roman historian Tacitus wrote a famous work literally called The Annals, which is a year-by-year account of events in the Roman Empire.

So in this strict sense: annals = a chronological, year-by-year written record.

The modern, everyday sense (which you will encounter far more often) has grown broader. Today, "annals" simply refers to the entire body of historical records and documented knowledge about something — a subject, a nation, an organization, a field of human activity, or all of human history itself. It no longer has to be strictly organized by year. It just means "the accumulated, documented history of."

Both senses point to the same core idea: a serious, written record of what has happened over time.
The most important phrase: "in the annals of..."

The single most common way you will encounter "annals" in real life is in the phrase "in the annals of [something]." The word following "of" can be almost anything — history, science, sport, medicine, literature, crime, music, war, art.

This phrase simply means: "in the recorded, documented history of that subject."

  • "Her discovery will go down in the annals of medicine as one of the greatest breakthroughs of the century."
  • "It was one of the most shameful chapters in the annals of warfare."
  • "His name is forever written in the annals of space exploration."

Here is something important that a dictionary definition alone might not tell you. When something is said to appear "in the annals of" something, it almost always implies that the thing is remarkable, memorable, or historically significant — for better or for worse. Nobody says, "in the annals of history, James went to the market." The word carries weight. It signals that what is being described is the kind of thing history actually bothers to remember and write down.

The word itself is completely neutral — it makes no judgment about whether an event is admirable or terrible. The annals of history contain both heroic achievements and horrific atrocities. Context tells you which is being referred to. But in either case, the word suggests that the event is historically notable.
It can refer to academic journals too

In scholarly and academic settings, you will sometimes see "Annals" used in the title of a professional journal or publication — for example, Annals of Surgery, Annals of Mathematics, or Annals of Internal Medicine. In these cases, the word signals that the publication is an authoritative, ongoing record of important developments in that field. This is a direct extension of the word's core meaning: a formal record of what is happening and what matters.
How it differs from similar words

Understanding what makes "annals" different from nearby words will lock its meaning in firmly.

History is the broader umbrella term for the past. "Annals" has a more formal, literary, record-keeping flavor. It specifically suggests something that has been written down and preserved, not just experienced or remembered.

Records is more general and everyday. "Annals" has a grander, more solemn feel. Records can be mundane (a record of purchases); annals are reserved for things of historical consequence.

Chronicles is the closest cousin to "annals" — both mean a record of events over time. The subtle difference is that chronicles tend to tell a story with a narrative flow, while annals emphasize the factual, structured documentation of events, often tied to time.

Archives refers to the physical or digital collection of stored documents and materials. "Annals" refers to the narrative record itself — the compiled history — not the place or system where documents are kept.

"Annals" means the formal, written record of significant historical events — whether of a particular year, a field of knowledge, an organization, a civilization, or all of humanity. It is nearly always plural, almost always appears in the phrase "in the annals of [something]," and carries the strong implication that whatever is being mentioned is noteworthy enough to belong in history's documented record. The word is neutral in tone but serious in weight — it is the kind of word you reach for when you want to say that something truly matters to history.
772:
To anneal something means to heat it to a very high temperature and then allow it to cool down very slowly and gradually. This is done deliberately, under controlled conditions, to make the material stronger, tougher, more flexible, and easier to work with.

The most common materials that are annealed are metals (like steel, copper, brass, and aluminum) and glass.

Imagine a metal rod. When you hammer it, bend it, or pull it into a wire, you're forcing its internal structure to change shape violently. The atoms inside get locked into stressed, strained positions — like a crowd of people who got shoved and are now standing awkwardly, bumping into each other. The metal becomes hard, yes, but also brittle — meaning it can crack or snap unexpectedly under pressure, because there's no "give" left in it.

Annealing solves this problem. When you heat the metal high enough, the atoms gain enough energy to move around and rearrange themselves into a calmer, more orderly, more stable pattern — like that same crowd finally relaxing and standing comfortably. Then, by cooling it slowly, you give them enough time to fully settle into that new, relaxed arrangement before the structure "freezes" again.

The result? A material that is:

  • Less brittle (it can bend without snapping)
  • Less internally stressed (the invisible tension is gone)
  • Softer and more ductile (easier to stretch, shape, or draw into thin wire)
  • More uniform internally (consistent properties throughout)
What "Slowly" Actually Means — And Why It Matters

The slow cooling is not accidental or just a side detail — it's the whole point.

If you heat metal and then cool it rapidly (by plunging it into cold water, for example — a process called quenching), the atoms don't have time to rearrange properly. They get "frozen" in place mid-rearrangement, creating a different kind of internal structure that is very hard but also very brittle. This is the opposite of what annealing achieves.

Annealing deliberately avoids this. The metal is often placed in a furnace or oven that is slowly turned down over many hours, or even days for large pieces. This gives atoms time to fully reorganize, relieve stress, and reach a low-energy, stable state before everything locks back into place as the metal cools.

In metalworking and manufacturing: A blacksmith or jeweller anneals copper wire to make it pliable again after working it. Steel parts in cars and machines are annealed to ensure they don't crack under stress. Surgical tools are annealed to combine toughness with workability.

In glassmaking: Raw glass straight from the furnace cools unevenly, which creates internal stress points that can cause it to crack or shatter spontaneously — even days later. Glass is annealed in a special oven called a lehr, where it is cooled at a precisely controlled, gradual rate to eliminate those stress points. Virtually all quality glass — windows, bottles, laboratory glassware — is annealed.

In electronics and semiconductors: Silicon wafers used in computer chips are annealed at various stages of manufacturing to repair damage, activate certain materials, or improve the electrical properties of the wafer.

Because annealing transforms something raw and stressed into something refined and resilient through the application of heat and time, the word is also used figuratively in writing and speech. When writers or speakers say that someone or something was annealed by hardship, adversity, or experience, they mean that going through that difficult process made the person or thing stronger, more durable, and more refined — the way fire and slow cooling strengthen steel.

For example: "Years of hardship had annealed her character into something quiet and unbreakable."

This figurative use is less common in everyday speech but appears regularly in literature, journalism, and formal writing.

There is also a well-known concept in computer science called simulated annealing, which is a problem-solving technique directly inspired by the physical process. Just as physical annealing finds the lowest-energy, most stable arrangement of atoms by slowly reducing temperature, the algorithm finds the best (most optimal) solution to a complex problem by starting with high "randomness" and slowly reducing it over time. The metaphor is deliberate and precise: the algorithm literally simulates the cooling curve of physical annealing to "settle" into an optimal answer rather than getting stuck at a merely good one.

To anneal is to deliberately heat a material — typically metal or glass — to a high temperature and then cool it very slowly, so that its internal structure can reorganize, its internal stresses can be relieved, and it becomes tougher, less brittle, and more workable.
773:
An annex is an addition to something that already exists — something secondary and supplementary, always attached to or associated with a main, primary thing. The annex is never the center of anything; it is always the extra.

The word is used primarily in two situations: buildings and documents.

This is by far the most common use. An annex is a building — or a part of a building — that is added on to a larger, main building, usually to provide more space. It might be physically connected to the main building, or it could be a separate but nearby structure that serves the same overall purpose.

Think of it this way: a school grows too large and runs out of space. Instead of rebuilding the whole school, the administration puts up a smaller, additional building right next door, dedicated to extra classrooms. That extra building is the school's annex. It isn't the school in the full sense — the original building is the school — but it belongs to the school and functions as part of it.

Other examples work the same way. A hospital that runs out of patient rooms might open an annex down the road for more beds. A busy government office might rent an extra building nearby as an annex for overflow staff. A museum might construct an annex to display more artwork.

A few things worth noticing about this sense of the word:

The annex is almost always the smaller or less important of the two structures. The main building comes first, both in time and in significance, and the annex comes after, as a response to need. You would never call the original, main building the annex — the word only belongs to the addition.

The annex is also always understood in relation to its main building. If you strip away the relationship, it's just a building. The word "annex" specifically signals that this structure is the secondary part of a larger whole — an extension of something bigger.

The word also appears regularly in formal, official documents — think international treaties, legal contracts, and government reports. In this context, an annex is a section added at the end of a main document that contains supplementary information. The core content lives in the main document; the supporting details, technical data, maps, or specifications that are too granular to include in the main text are placed in the annex.

Imagine a trade agreement signed between two countries. The main agreement lays out the broad terms: what goods will be traded, what the overall rules are, how disputes will be handled. But attached at the very end, you might find pages and pages listing exact product codes, precise numerical quotas, and detailed technical definitions. Those attached pages form the annex (or annexes, since there can be more than one). They're too specific and detailed for the main text, but they're still a formal and necessary part of the full document.

This use of the word is quite similar to the word "appendix," which you may already know. The two words overlap considerably, but "appendix" tends to appear in academic writing and books, while "annex" is the preferred term in legal, governmental, and international contexts.
The single idea that connects all of this

No matter the context — building or document — the word annex carries the exact same underlying idea: it is something that has been added onto something else. It is always secondary, always supplementary, always pointing back toward a main thing that it belongs to and extends.

When you encounter the word "annex," you can confidently read it as: the extra part of something larger. It is not the core — it is the complement to the core. And critically, it only makes sense in the presence of that main thing. A building is just a building until it becomes an annex to something else; at that point, its very identity is defined by its relationship to what came before it.

That relationship — between the main thing and its addition — is what the word "annex" is fundamentally about.
774:
To annex something means to take control of a place or territory and permanently absorb it into your own country, state, or domain — making it officially "yours."

Think of it like this: if you swallow something, it stops being a separate thing and becomes part of you. Annexing a territory is the political equivalent of that. The annexed land stops being independent and becomes a formal part of the annexing country.

The word "annex" isn't just about entering or occupying a place. It carries a very specific, decisive meaning:

  • It is a declaration of permanent ownership. You're not just visiting, controlling, or occupying — you're saying "this now belongs to us."
  • It is a political and legal act. The annexing power formally incorporates the territory into its own legal and administrative system. The annexed land gets governed by the annexing country's laws.
  • It is usually done by a more powerful entity over a weaker one. A small town doesn't annex a superpower. It flows in one direction — strength absorbing weakness.

This is where most learners miss the depth of the word, so pay close attention.

1. Annexation ≠ Invasion
An invasion is the military act of entering someone's territory by force. An annexation is the political act of claiming that territory as your own. They often happen together, but they are not the same thing. A country can invade without annexing (e.g., entering a country to fight a war, then withdrawing). And technically, annexation can even happen without a military invasion — through political pressure, treaties, or coercion. Invasion is the means; annexation is the outcome.

2. Annexation ≠ Occupation
Occupation means you are controlling a territory militarily, but you have not formally claimed it as yours. It is understood — even by the occupying power — to be a temporary arrangement. Annexation removes that "temporary" quality. It says: we are not leaving, and this is now ours forever.

3. Annexation ≠ Colonization
Colonization refers to a broader process of settling, exploiting, and dominating a foreign land — often over long periods, involving cultural and economic control. Annexation is a specific legal/political act within a moment in time. Colonization can include annexation, but annexation by itself doesn't mean colonization.

4. Consent is rarely part of the picture
In almost every real-world use of this word, the territory being annexed has not agreed to it. The people living there may strongly object. This is why annexation is almost always controversial, and why it carries a weight of aggression, illegitimacy, or injustice in most modern contexts. Under international law today, annexing territory by force is considered illegal and a violation of a nation's sovereignty.

These examples will cement the word firmly in your mind.

  • Russia annexing Crimea (2014): Russia sent military forces into the Crimean Peninsula (which was part of Ukraine) and then formally declared Crimea to be Russian territory. This is a textbook modern example of annexation — territory was absorbed into Russia against Ukraine's will and against international law. Most of the world refused to recognise it.
  • Nazi Germany annexing Austria (1938): Germany formally merged Austria into the German Reich, calling it Anschluss (meaning "joining"). Austria ceased to exist as an independent country and was absorbed into Germany.
  • The United States annexing Texas (1845): After Texas declared independence from Mexico and spent years as its own republic, the U.S. formally annexed it — incorporating it as the 28th U.S. state. Texas went from being a separate nation to being American territory.
  • The United States annexing Hawaii (1898): The U.S. formally annexed the Hawaiian Islands, which led to Hawaii eventually becoming a U.S. state in 1959. This annexation is historically controversial because it involved the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy.

These examples reveal a pattern: the word almost always comes up in the context of powerful nations expanding their borders by absorbing lands that didn't originally belong to them.

While "annex" is most commonly used for territories and countries, it can also be applied more broadly:

  • A large city can annex a smaller neighboring town — taking it into its municipal boundaries so it is governed as part of the city. This is very common in urban expansion.
  • In informal or figurative language, you might hear someone say a large company "annexed" a smaller firm's resources or technology — meaning it absorbed them completely and made them its own.

These uses carry the same core idea: take something separate and pull it fully into your own domain.
The Feel and Weight of the Word

One final thing that will make you a truly precise user of this word: "annex" is not a neutral word. It carries weight. When you say a country annexed a territory, you are implying that the original occupants or the previous owner did not fully consent, and that the act was unilateral — done by the annexing power on its own terms. Writers, journalists, and historians choose this word deliberately to signal that kind of forceful, one-sided absorption.

If a territory voluntarily joined another country through a democratic vote and a mutual agreement, you'd be more likely to use words like merged with, unified with, or joined — not annexed.

To annex is to formally and permanently absorb a territory into your own country or domain, typically without the consent of those being absorbed, and in a way that makes it legally and politically yours from that point forward.
775:
Annexation is the act of one country, government, or authority formally taking over a territory and making it their own, permanently and officially. Think of it as one entity reaching out, grabbing a piece of land that was previously separate or belonged to someone else, and declaring: "This is now part of us."

The key word is formally. Annexation is not just physically controlling a place — it is officially and legally absorbing it into your own territory, changing its status on the map, and treating it as a permanent part of your own land.

Imagine you own a house, and the house next to yours is either unoccupied, disputed, or belongs to a weaker neighbor. One day, you put up a fence around their yard, declare it yours, give it your address, and start making rules for it as if it were always your property. You didn't buy it through a mutual agreement. You just took it and made it yours by declaration. That is essentially what annexation is — just at a political and governmental scale, involving territories, states, or countries.
What Makes Annexation Different From Similar Ideas

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Annexation vs. Occupation. When a military force moves into and controls a foreign territory during a conflict, that is called occupation. It is temporary and does not change who the land legally belongs to. Annexation goes one step further — it is a formal declaration that the land now permanently belongs to the annexing power. Russia militarily occupied parts of Ukraine, and then formally annexed them — that second step is what makes it annexation, not just occupation.

Annexation vs. Conquest. Conquest is the act of winning control over a territory, usually through war. Annexation is what often follows conquest — the official paperwork, the declaration, the formal absorption. Conquest is the deed; annexation is the claim that follows.

Annexation vs. Merger or Unification. A merger or unification typically involves mutual agreement between two parties who both want to join together. Annexation, by contrast, is almost always one-sided — the stronger party decides, and the other side rarely has a meaningful choice. When two equals voluntarily combine, it is a union. When one forces the other in, it is annexation.
The Two Main Contexts Where This Word Is Used

1. International and Political Annexation

This is the most common and significant use of the word. It refers to one country formally absorbing the territory of another country or a disputed region. This is serious business in world affairs because it changes national borders, affects the people living there (their citizenship, rights, laws), and can trigger international conflict.

Famous examples include:

  • Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, when Russia formally declared that the Crimean Peninsula — which was part of Ukraine — was now Russian territory. Most of the world did not recognize this as legal.
  • Germany's annexation of Austria in 1938, known historically as the Anschluss, when Nazi Germany absorbed Austria into the German Reich.
  • The United States' annexation of Texas in 1845, when the Republic of Texas — which had declared independence from Mexico — was formally incorporated as a U.S. state.
  • Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 and the Golan Heights, both of which are disputed and not recognized by most of the international community.

2. Municipal or Administrative Annexation

This is a quieter, more everyday use of the word, but it follows the same logic. Cities and towns regularly annex nearby land — suburbs, rural areas, or neighboring communities — to expand their official boundaries. When a growing city in the United States absorbs a surrounding township into its city limits, that is annexation too. The city now governs that land, collects taxes from it, and provides it with city services. This type of annexation is usually done through legal and administrative processes, and is far less controversial than the international kind.
The Question of Legality and Recognition

One of the most important things to understand about annexation is that doing it and having the world accept it are two very different things. A country can declare annexation, but other countries and international bodies like the United Nations can — and often do — refuse to recognize it as valid or legal.

Under modern international law, particularly the United Nations Charter, it is considered illegal to annex another country's territory by force. This principle is called the inadmissibility of acquisition of territory by war. The reasoning is straightforward: if powerful nations were allowed to simply seize weaker nations' lands whenever they won a military conflict, the world would have no stability, no rule of law, and smaller nations would have no security.

This is why you will often hear phrases like "unrecognized annexation" or "illegal annexation" in news reports. The annexing country considers the land theirs; the rest of the world disagrees and continues to treat the original borders as legitimate. This creates a contested situation that can persist for decades or even longer.

That said, historically — before modern international law developed — annexation was extremely common and widely accepted as a normal consequence of war and empire-building. The Roman Empire, the Mongol Empire, the British Empire, and virtually every major power in history expanded through annexation. The moral and legal judgment placed on annexation is largely a product of the 20th century's effort to build a more rules-based international order.
The Effect on the People Living There

Annexation is not just about maps and borders — it profoundly affects real people. When a territory is annexed, the people living in it may suddenly find themselves under a completely different government, with different laws, a different official language being imposed, different citizenship rules, and different rights. They may be welcomed as citizens, treated as subjects, or persecuted — depending on the nature of the annexing power. This human dimension is why annexation, especially when done by force, is often considered a serious injustice.

Annexation is the formal, official act of taking over and permanently absorbing a territory into your own country, city, or governing authority. It is one-sided, it changes who governs a place and who it legally "belongs" to, and it can be either legally recognized (as in peaceful municipal expansion) or broadly condemned (as in forcible seizure of another country's land). It has shaped empires, caused wars, displaced populations, and continues to be one of the most consequential and controversial acts in world politics.
776:
To annihilate something means to destroy it so completely that it effectively ceases to exist. Not just damage it. Not just break it. But wipe it out entirely — leaving nothing, or next to nothing, behind.

Think of the difference between crumpling a piece of paper and burning it to ash. Crumpling damages it. Burning annihilates it. The paper is simply gone.

This idea of total, absolute, zero-trace destruction is the heart of this word.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Literal / Physical Destruction

When used literally, "annihilate" describes the complete physical destruction of something — a place, an army, a population, or even matter itself.

  • A nuclear bomb can annihilate an entire city.
  • The meteor impact was so powerful that it annihilated every living thing in the region.
  • In physics, when a particle meets its antiparticle (its exact opposite), they annihilate each other — both vanish completely, converting into pure energy. This is a precise scientific use of the word.

Notice that in all of these cases, what is destroyed doesn't just become "broken" — it is gone.

2. Figurative / Non-Physical Destruction

This is where the word gets really interesting and is perhaps most commonly used in everyday life. You don't need a bomb to annihilate something. The word is used figuratively to describe:

a) Crushing defeat
When one person, team, or side defeats another so overwhelmingly that the loser had absolutely no chance, you can say they were annihilated.

  • Our football team annihilated the opponents 9–0.
  • She annihilated her rival in the debate — he couldn't answer a single point.

The key here is the scale of the defeat. A narrow win is not annihilation. It has to be a total, humiliating, one-sided destruction.

b) Destroying ideas, arguments, or reputations
You can also annihilate something that isn't physical at all — like a theory, a claim, or someone's confidence.

  • The scientist's new data annihilated the old theory that had been accepted for decades.
  • The brutal review annihilated his reputation as a writer.
  • Her sharp response annihilated his argument before he could finish making it.

Here, the "destruction" is intellectual or emotional — but it is still total. The argument doesn't just get weakened; it gets demolished beyond recovery.

The single most important thing that separates "annihilate" from weaker words like damage, harm, beat, or even destroy is its absoluteness.

  • To damage something = it still exists, just hurt.
  • To destroy something = it is broken apart, possibly beyond repair.
  • To annihilate something = it is obliterated. Gone. No remnants. No recovery.

Whenever you use or read this word, that sense of finality and completeness is always present. Nothing survives annihilation.

"Annihilate" is a strong, dramatic word. Because of this:

  • It is often used for emphasis — to make a point feel more powerful than a plain word would.
  • It carries a tone that is intense and serious in literal contexts, but can also be used playfully or humorously in casual speech (e.g., "I just annihilated that pizza" meaning you ate it very fast and completely).
  • It is not a word you would use for small, minor destructions. You would not say "the rain annihilated my umbrella." That would feel exaggerated to the point of being wrong. The scale of what is being destroyed should always justify the word.

The subject doing the annihilating can be almost anything:

  • A person → "She annihilated her competition."
  • A weapon or force of nature → "The tsunami annihilated the coastal village."
  • An idea or piece of evidence → "This proof annihilates the conspiracy theory."
  • A team or army → "The invading force annihilated the defenders."

And what gets annihilated can be:

  • A physical place, army, or object
  • A person's confidence, reputation, or argument
  • A theory, belief, or claim
  • An opponent in a game, sport, or competition

Knowing related words will make this one stick even better:

  • Annihilation (noun) → the act or result of annihilating: "The annihilation of the enemy army took just three days."
  • Annihilated (past tense / adjective) → "The town was completely annihilated."
  • Annihilating (present participle) → "They are annihilating every team they face."

AspectDetail

Annihilate means to destroy something so completely that it is essentially wiped out of existence. Literally, it refers to total physical destruction. Figuratively, it refers to an overwhelming defeat or the complete dismantling of an idea, argument, or reputation. The word always implies totality — not partial damage, but utter and complete obliteration. It is a strong, dramatic word, so it should be used when the scale of destruction genuinely warrants it.
777:
Annihilation means the complete and total destruction of something — so thorough that it leaves nothing behind. It comes from the verb annihilate, and when you turn it into a noun, it names the act, event, or result of that total destruction.

The key idea is nothingness. Not just damage. Not just defeat. Not even ordinary destruction. Annihilation means something is wiped out of existence so completely that it is essentially reduced to nothing.
Why This Word is Stronger Than "Destruction"

English has many words for destroying things, and they exist on a scale of severity. Understanding where annihilation sits on that scale is crucial.

Damage → something is harmed but still exists and can recover.
Destruction → something is broken down badly, often beyond repair.
Obliteration → something is erased, leaving almost no trace.
Annihilation → something is eliminated so completely that it simply ceases to exist.

Annihilation is the most extreme end of that scale. If a building is destroyed, you might still find rubble. If it is annihilated, the idea is that even the rubble is gone — there is nothing left to point to. This is why the word carries such enormous emotional and intellectual weight. It signals absolute finality.

In its most direct, physical sense, annihilation refers to the complete wiping out of something real and tangible.

When used in warfare or conflict, it describes the total elimination of an enemy force — not just defeating them, but destroying them so thoroughly that they have no ability to recover or even exist anymore. "The annihilation of the opposing army ended the war." Here, the army isn't just beaten — it is gone.

It can also describe the destruction of a place. "The annihilation of the ancient city left no stone standing." No ruins, no survivors, no trace — just absence.

In physics, the word has a very specific and precise scientific meaning. When a particle of matter meets its corresponding particle of anti-matter (its exact opposite), the two collide and completely destroy each other. They are converted entirely into pure energy — neither particle survives. Scientists call this event annihilation. It is one of the few contexts in human knowledge where something is literally converted into nothing (or more accurately, into pure energy, leaving no physical matter behind). This is the most scientifically exact use of the word.

Because the word is so powerful, people also use it in non-physical, metaphorical ways to describe situations where something non-tangible is utterly destroyed.

Annihilation of hope: When someone's dreams or hopes are completely crushed — not just dimmed, but extinguished entirely — you might say there was an annihilation of hope. "The rejection letter brought the annihilation of everything she had worked toward."

Annihilation of a reputation: If a person's good name or credibility is completely destroyed by a scandal, leaving nothing positive behind, that can be called the annihilation of their reputation.

Annihilation in competition: In sports or debates, if one side completely dominates the other and leaves them with nothing — no points, no arguments, no dignity — the loss can be described as an annihilation. "The team suffered annihilation on the field, losing 12–0." This is a hyperbolic but widely understood use.

Annihilation of an idea or argument: If someone dismantles an argument so completely that not a single part of it survives, they might be said to have caused its annihilation. "His annihilation of their theory left the scientific community speechless."

Beyond its definition, annihilation carries a tone of absolute, irreversible finality. When you use this word, you are signaling that there is no going back, no recovery, no remnant. It often carries a weight of dread, awe, or shock — because total elimination is a profound and unsettling concept for human beings.

This is why the word appears so often in serious contexts: wars, existential threats, scientific extremes, and devastating personal losses. It is not a casual word. You would not say "I annihilated my sandwich" in everyday speech without it sounding theatrical or humorous, precisely because the word is so disproportionately large for something small.

It implies no survivors and no remnants. Ordinary destruction can leave wreckage. Annihilation, by definition, does not. Even if in practice some small trace remains, the word communicates the intent or result of leaving nothing behind.

It implies irreversibility. You can rebuild after destruction. You cannot rebuild after true annihilation, because there is nothing left to rebuild from. This is one of the most important distinctions.

It can be used literally or figuratively, but both uses carry equal seriousness. Whether you're describing a nuclear event or the collapse of someone's confidence, the word signals that whatever happened was complete and final.

The scale of what is annihilated can vary. A single soldier can face annihilation. So can an entire civilization. So can a subatomic particle. The word does not require a large subject — it requires total elimination of whatever the subject is, regardless of size.
Quick Mental Image to Remember It

Imagine writing something on a piece of paper. Now imagine:

  • Damaging it = crumpling it.
  • Destroying it = tearing it into pieces.
  • Obliterating it = burning it to ash.
  • Annihilation = the ash itself disappears. There is nothing — not even dust — left to show the paper ever existed.

That is annihilation.

Annihilation is a noun that means the act or result of something being completely and totally destroyed — reduced to nothing, with no trace, no survivors, and no possibility of recovery. It is the most extreme form of destruction in the English language, used both literally (in warfare, physics, and catastrophe) and figuratively (in competition, emotion, and ideas). It always communicates absolute, irreversible finality.
778:
An anniversary is a day that comes back every year on the exact same date as a meaningful past event. The idea is simple: something important happened on a specific date, and every year when that date returns, it is called the anniversary of that event.

For example, if two people got married on August 28, 2020, then every August 28 after that is their wedding anniversary. If a country was founded on July 4, 1776, then every July 4 after that is the anniversary of its founding. The word works equally for personal moments and for large historical events.

An anniversary almost always carries a count — the number of years that have passed since the original event. This is why you hear phrases like "our 5th anniversary," "the 50th anniversary of the moon landing," or "the 100th anniversary of the city's founding." The count tells you exactly how long ago the original event took place.
What kinds of events can have an anniversary?

Almost any significant event can have one. The most common types are wedding anniversaries, which couples celebrate each year after getting married; founding anniversaries, which businesses, schools, cities, and countries mark to honor the date they were established; historical anniversaries, which are used to remember major events like wars, treaties, or discoveries; and death anniversaries, which are observed to honor and remember someone who has passed away. There is no strict rule about what counts — it simply needs to be an event meaningful enough to remember on a yearly basis.
The mood is not always celebratory

An anniversary is not always a joyful occasion. Wedding and founding anniversaries are typically celebrated with happiness, but the anniversary of a death or a tragedy is usually a quiet, solemn time for remembrance. The word itself carries no emotional judgment — it simply marks the return of a date. Whether people celebrate or grieve depends entirely on the nature of the original event.

Some anniversaries, especially wedding ones, have long-standing traditional names in English based on the number of years. The most well-known ones are the silver anniversary for the 25th year, the golden anniversary for the 50th year, and the diamond anniversary for the 60th year. Others include the paper anniversary for the 1st year, the wood anniversary for the 5th, the tin or aluminum anniversary for the 10th, the crystal anniversary for the 15th, the china anniversary for the 20th, the pearl anniversary for the 30th, the ruby anniversary for the 40th, and the platinum anniversary for the 70th. These names are widely recognized in English-speaking cultures, though they are used most commonly for wedding milestones.
How it is used in sentences

"They celebrated their 20th wedding anniversary in Paris."
"The company is marking its 100th anniversary this year."
"He lit a candle on the anniversary of his mother's death."
"The president spoke on the 50th anniversary of the peace treaty."
"Today is the 30th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall."

The verbs most naturally paired with anniversary are celebrate, mark, observe, and commemorate. You celebrate a joyful anniversary, mark or observe a solemn one, and commemorate a significant historical one.

This is a distinction learners often find confusing. A birthday refers only to the date on which a specific person or animal was born. An anniversary, by contrast, can refer to the yearly return of any kind of significant event — which may include a birth, but also a marriage, a death, a founding, or a historical moment. In everyday English, you say "my birthday" for the day you were born. However, if you are talking about a famous person from history, you might say "the 200th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's birth." For living people, "birthday" is always the natural and correct word to use.

Since the word "anniversary" already means something that returns every year, saying "annual anniversary" is technically redundant — it is like saying "yearly yearly return." However, people do say it in casual speech sometimes, and it is understood without any confusion.

In short, an anniversary is the yearly return of the date of a past event — personal or historical, joyful or solemn — and it always tells you both what happened and how long ago it happened.
779: At its most essential, to annotate means to add your own notes, comments, or explanations to a piece of content — a book, a document, an image, a piece of code, anything — without changing the original content itself. The notes you add are called annotations.
The Core Idea: You Are Adding, Not Changing

This is the single most important thing to understand. When you annotate something, the original stays exactly as it is. Your notes sit alongside it — pointing to it, explaining it, questioning it, or commenting on it — but never replacing or altering it. This is what separates annotating from editing, where you actually change the original words.

Picture a student reading a dense history textbook. She comes across a confusing paragraph, so she writes a small explanation in the margin. She circles an important date and jots down why it matters. She draws an arrow connecting two ideas on different parts of the page. She has just annotated the book. The original text is untouched. She has simply added a personal layer of notes on top of it.

The form of an annotation changes depending on where you're working, but the act is always the same.

In a physical book, annotations are the notes scribbled in the margins, the underlined sentences with brief comments beside them, the question marks next to confusing passages, or the small stars marking something important.

In a digital document like a Google Doc or a Word file, annotations appear as comment bubbles that float alongside the text, attached to a specific word or paragraph — without disturbing the document itself.

In computer programming, annotations are the lines a programmer writes inside their code to explain what the code is doing. The computer ignores these lines; they are purely for human readers.

On a map or scientific diagram, annotations are the labels and notes added to identify or explain specific regions or features.

In academic writing, annotations often appear as footnotes or endnotes — small numbered references at the bottom of a page or at the end of a document that provide extra context or explanation for something in the main text.

To understand better. Writing a note next to a difficult passage forces your brain to actually process what you've read. This is why teachers tell students to annotate while studying — the act of forming a note deepens your comprehension.

To remember. When you return to a document weeks later, your annotations act as breadcrumbs. They help you instantly recall what was important and why, without having to re-read everything.

To give feedback. An editor annotates a manuscript to point out issues to the author. A professor annotates a student's essay to suggest improvements. The original work stays intact; the notes are a conversation layered on top of it.

To analyse or critique. Scholars annotate texts to examine them deeply — noting literary devices, historical references, logical flaws, or recurring themes. Annotating is how serious, close reading looks in practice.

In technology and artificial intelligence. This is a major modern use of the word. In machine learning, "annotating data" means labelling raw information so that computers can learn from it. For example, if you look at thousands of photos and draw a box around every dog and label it "dog," you are annotating that image dataset. The AI then uses those human-made labels to learn how to recognise dogs on its own. Data annotation is now an entire profession.

In law. Lawyers and legal scholars annotate statutes — written laws — with notes explaining how courts have interpreted those laws over time. An "annotated code" is a legal book that contains not just the law itself, but years of explanatory notes layered around it.
How It Looks in a Sentence

"The professor asked students to annotate the poem before the next class."

"I always annotate PDF articles when I'm doing research."

"Programmers annotate their code so other developers can understand it easily."

"The team spent three weeks annotating thousands of images for the AI training model."

"She returned to the book and found her old annotations still scrawled in the margins."
How It Differs from Words That Seem Similar

Annotate vs. comment: "Comment" is broader and more casual — you can comment on anything, verbally or in writing. "Annotate" is more specific and deliberate: it means adding written notes to a document or piece of content, usually in a structured way that is linked to specific parts of it.

Annotate vs. edit: Editing means changing or improving the original content. Annotating means adding notes without touching the original. An editor changes your words; an annotator adds remarks about them.

Annotate vs. highlight: Highlighting is simply marking something visually. Annotating goes further — it means writing something to explain, question, or comment on what you've marked. A highlight is silent; an annotation speaks.

Annotate vs. summarise: Summarising means condensing an entire piece into a shorter version. Annotating means adding specific notes at particular points within the piece. A summary stands alone; annotations live inside the original.

Annotation (noun) — the note itself, or the act of adding notes. "The margins were filled with annotations."

Annotated (adjective) — describes something that has had notes added to it. "An annotated edition of the novel." "An annotated bibliography."

Annotating (present participle) — the ongoing act. "She spent the afternoon annotating the report."

Annotator (noun) — a person who annotates. "The annotators labelled over 10,000 images for the dataset."
To annotate is to add explanatory or critical notes to a piece of content — text, image, code, or data — in a way that enriches or comments on it, while leaving the original completely intact.
780:
An annotation is a note, comment, or explanation that is added to a piece of existing content — such as a book, a document, an image, a piece of code, or a dataset — in order to explain, clarify, describe, or add information about that content.

The single most important thing to understand about the word is this: an annotation is always secondary. It is never the original content. It is something that gets layered on top of or alongside the original, without replacing or altering it. The original content exists first; the annotation comes after, as an addition.

Imagine you are reading a history textbook. You come across a sentence that mentions "The Treaty of Versailles" but doesn't explain what it is. Your teacher has already read this book and written a short note in the margin: "This was the peace agreement signed in 1919 after World War I."

That note in the margin is an annotation. It doesn't change what the book says. It simply sits beside the original text and gives you more information to help you understand it.

That is the essence of an annotation — a helpful addition attached to something, pointing at something specific within it, and saying more about it.

Annotations exist to serve several related purposes, and understanding these helps you grasp the full weight of the word:

To explain or clarify. When a part of the original content is difficult, technical, or ambiguous, an annotation breaks it down into simpler terms. A footnote at the bottom of a legal document that explains what a complicated clause means is an annotation doing this job.

To provide context. Sometimes the original content is clear on its own, but knowing the background makes it richer or more useful. A note attached to a historical photograph that reads "Taken during the Great Depression, 1932, New York City" is giving context. That note is an annotation.

To label or categorize. In some fields, especially in science and technology, annotations are used to tag or label specific things so that others can find, sort, or understand them easily. A scientist might annotate a gene in a genome sequence to indicate what that gene does.

To express a reaction, critique, or opinion. A reader who writes "I disagree with this argument" next to a paragraph in a book is annotating it — adding their own perspective as a note tied to that specific part of the text.

To cross-reference. An annotation might point you toward another source, saying in effect: "If you want to learn more about this, see page 47" or "Compare this with Chapter 5."
Where you encounter annotations in everyday life

The concept shows up in many different places, and recognizing it across these contexts is important:

In books and printed texts. This is the oldest and most familiar form. Annotations in books are the handwritten or printed notes found in margins (called marginal notes), at the bottom of a page (footnotes), or at the end of a chapter or book (endnotes). When a book is published with expert notes already built in — to help readers understand a difficult classic, for example — it is called an annotated edition or annotated version. The annotations in such a book might explain old words, historical references, or cultural context that a modern reader might not know.

In digital documents. When you use a program like Google Docs, Microsoft Word, or a PDF reader and you leave a comment on a specific part of the text, you are creating an annotation. The original document stays unchanged; your comment floats beside it, attached to the exact spot you highlighted.

In code (programming). Programmers routinely add short notes within their code to explain what different sections do. These are called annotations (or sometimes "comments," a word used interchangeably in this context). They are meant for other programmers — or for the same programmer returning to the code later — and are typically ignored by the computer when the code runs.

In science and research. Scientists annotate diagrams, images, and data constantly. A labeled diagram of the human heart — with arrows pointing to each part and the name written beside it — is an annotated diagram. Each label is an annotation.

In machine learning and artificial intelligence. This is a modern and increasingly important use. Before an AI can learn to recognize objects in photos or understand spoken language, humans must go through thousands of images or recordings and label them. A person who looks at a photo and types "this is a cat" is annotating that image. This process is called data annotation, and it is how AI systems are trained.

In law and official documents. Legal texts are often dense and hard to understand. Annotations are added — sometimes by publishers, sometimes by legal experts — to explain what each clause means, how courts have interpreted it, and what its practical effects are. A heavily annotated legal code is a common reference tool for lawyers.
What makes an annotation distinct from a simple "note"

This is a subtle but important distinction. A note is a general word — it can stand entirely on its own, independent of anything else. A shopping list, a diary entry, a reminder you wrote to yourself — these are all notes.

An annotation, however, is always attached to and dependent upon something else. It cannot exist in isolation in a meaningful way, because its entire purpose is to refer to, explain, or add information about a specific piece of existing content. Detach an annotation from what it is annotating and it often loses its meaning. The annotation "This refers to the 1814 battle" means nothing by itself — you need to know what "this" is pointing to.

So the key difference is one of attachment and dependency: an annotation always belongs to something; a note can stand alone.
A note on the difference between "annotation" and "comment"

In many everyday contexts, these two words are used interchangeably, and that is perfectly acceptable. However, "annotation" tends to carry a slightly more formal, deliberate, or scholarly tone. When someone says "I added a comment," it can feel casual and spontaneous. When someone says "I added an annotation," it suggests a more intentional act — typically one meant to inform, explain, or enrich the content it is attached to, often in a structured or systematic way.

In technical fields like software engineering or data science, the two words sometimes have distinct, precise meanings defined by the tools being used — but in general language, they overlap heavily.

An annotation is any note, label, explanation, or comment that is deliberately added to an existing piece of content — text, image, code, data, or otherwise — in order to explain, clarify, contextualize, label, or enrich that content. It is always secondary to the original; it adds to it without replacing it. It is always attached to something specific within the original content, pointing at it and saying something more about it. You encounter annotations in books, digital documents, scientific diagrams, legal texts, programming code, and AI training data. The act of creating annotations is called annotating, and a piece of content that has had annotations added to it is described as annotated.
781:
To announce something means to make information known to people — usually publicly, officially, or to a group — often for the first time.

When you announce something, you are not just quietly telling one person in private. You are sharing news with an audience, whether that audience is a room full of people, a whole country, or the general public. There is almost always a sense that the information is new, important, and meant to be heard by more than just one person.

Think of it this way: if you whisper a secret to your best friend, that is not announcing. But if you stand up at a dinner table and say "I have some news for everyone!" — that is announcing.

The word carries three key qualities that set it apart from simply "saying" or "telling" something:

1. It is directed at an audience (not just one person).
An announcement is meant for a group — a crowd, a company, the public, or at least a defined set of people. Even if only one person is in the room, "announcing" suggests the message has a wider reach or importance.

2. It carries a sense of officiality or significance.
When something is announced, it usually feels formal, deliberate, or important. You don't "announce" that you want a glass of water. You announce a decision, a result, a plan, or a piece of major news.

3. The information is typically new.
Announcing something implies that the people hearing it are learning about it for the first time. It is a revelation of new information, not a reminder of something already known.
The Many Situations Where "Announce" Is Used

"Announce" is a flexible word used in many different real-life situations.

Personal news:

  • A couple stands before their family and announces their engagement.
  • A woman announces to her friends that she is expecting a baby.

Official or organizational news:

  • A company announces that it is launching a new product.
  • A government announces a change in policy.
  • A school announces that classes will be cancelled due to snow.

Results and decisions:

  • The judges announced the winner of the competition.
  • The committee announced its final decision after months of debate.

Arrivals and events:

  • A flight attendant announces that the plane is about to land.
  • A receptionist announces that your guest has arrived.
  • The host announces the start of the ceremony.

Media and public communication:

  • A news channel announces breaking news.
  • A company announces its quarterly earnings to investors.

There is no single method. You can announce something:

  • By speaking aloud in front of people
  • Through a written statement or press release
  • On television, radio, or the internet
  • Through a loudspeaker or public address system
  • In a letter or official document

What matters is not how you do it, but the intention: making information known to people in a deliberate, clear, and often formal way.

"Announce" works in several grammatical patterns:

announce + noun (thing being announced):

The president announced his resignation.
The team announced the new signing.

announce + that + a full sentence:

The company announced that it would be closing two of its offices.
She announced that she had won the award.

announce + to + a person/group:

The manager announced to the staff that salaries would increase next year.
He announced to the world that he was retiring.

In passive voice (something is announced):

The results were announced yesterday.
A new law has been announced by the government.

It helps to understand what this word does not cover:

  • It does not mean a casual, private mention. If you text a friend "hey, I got a new job," you are not announcing it — you are simply telling them.
  • It does not mean gossiping or sharing information without the speaker's authority or intention.
  • It does not mean spreading a rumor — an announcement is deliberate and usually made by someone who has the authority or right to share that information.

These words are related but not exactly the same:

  • Tell — private, one person to another, informal. "I told my sister the news."
  • Inform — official but often private; you inform a specific person. "We will inform you of the decision by email."
  • Declare — very strong and emphatic; often used for grand or official statements. "The president declared a state of emergency."
  • Proclaim — very formal and public; often used by leaders or in historical contexts. "The king proclaimed his victory."
  • Announce — sits in the middle: public, deliberate, significant, but everyday enough to use in both casual and formal contexts.

The key difference: "announce" always implies a group is being informed, and the news is being shared openly and deliberately.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Go With "Announce")

Certain words appear together with "announce" very frequently:

  • Officially announce — to make it formal and definitive
  • Publicly announce — to make it known to the public
  • Proudly announce — to share good news with happiness
  • Formally announce — to declare in an official setting
  • Announce a decision / a plan / a policy — sharing an official choice
  • Announce a winner / the results — revealing an outcome
  • Announce a resignation / retirement / departure — sharing the news of someone leaving

When someone announces something, there is often a built-in sense of ceremony. The speaker is saying, in effect: "Stop and listen. What I am about to say matters, and it is meant for all of you."

This is why "announce" is used at weddings ("It is my honor to announce the newlyweds!"), at press conferences, at award shows, and at the start of important meetings. The word itself signals: this is a moment worth paying attention to.
To announce something is to deliberately and openly make a piece of important news known to a group of people, often for the first time, in a way that feels deliberate, clear, and significant.
782:
To annoy someone means to cause them a feeling of mild irritation, impatience, or displeasure. When you annoy someone, you make them feel bothered — not deeply hurt, not furious, but uncomfortable in a nagging, "I wish this would stop" kind of way.

Think of it like a fly buzzing near your ear. It is not dangerous. It does not cause serious pain. But it keeps bothering you, and you cannot ignore it. That is the feeling of being annoyed.
The Emotional Level — How Strong Is It?

This is one of the most important things to understand about "annoy." It describes a mild to moderate level of emotional discomfort. It is not a heavy word.

Picture a scale of emotional disturbance:

Bother → Annoy → Irritate → Upset → Anger → Infuriate

"Annoy" sits on the lighter end of this scale. It does not mean to make someone deeply sad, traumatized, or explosively angry. If a sound annoys you, you feel impatient and wish it would stop. You have not been wounded or destroyed by it.

That said, something that annoys you repeatedly over time can eventually make you genuinely angry. The annoyance builds up. But the act of "annoying" itself points to that mild, persistent discomfort — not the final explosion.

This is wonderfully flexible. Almost anything can be the subject of "annoy":

A person can annoy another person:

My brother annoys me when he talks too loudly on the phone.

A thing (sound, smell, habit) can annoy someone:

The constant dripping of the tap annoys the entire family.

A situation or fact can annoy someone:

It annoys me that the bus is always late.

Notice in that last example the structure: "It annoys me that..." — this is extremely common in English and very natural. You are not annoyed by a person; you are annoyed by a situation or circumstance.

One subtle but crucial point: you can annoy someone completely by accident, without any intention. The word does not require the "annoyer" to be doing it on purpose.

The dog's barking annoys the neighbors. (The dog has no intention — but the effect is real.)

She did not mean to, but her habit of repeating herself annoyed her colleagues.

However, annoy can also describe deliberate behavior:

He knew she was trying to study, but he kept interrupting her just to annoy her.

So the word works in both directions — accidental and deliberate. What matters is the effect on the person being annoyed, not the intention behind it.

Learning the patterns will help you use "annoy" naturally:

1. [Subject] annoys [person]:

Loud music annoys me.

2. [Subject] annoys [person] by [doing something]:

He annoys his roommate by leaving dishes in the sink.

3. It annoys [person] that/when...:

It annoys her when people don't say "thank you."
It annoys me that nobody told me about the meeting.

4. [Person] is annoyed by [something] — passive form:

She was annoyed by the constant interruptions.

5. [Person] finds [something] annoying:

I find his attitude really annoying.
Do you find it annoying when people are late?
Words That Are Similar — And How They Differ

Irritate — Nearly identical to "annoy" in meaning. Slightly more formal. Often used for physical irritation too (a chemical can irritate your skin). When used emotionally, it is interchangeable with "annoy" in most situations, though "irritate" can sometimes imply a slightly sharper or more persistent feeling.

Bother — Slightly softer and more general than "annoy." To bother someone can mean to disturb, trouble, or mildly annoy them. "Sorry to bother you" is much gentler than "Sorry to annoy you."

Bug (informal) — A casual, everyday synonym for annoy.

It really bugs me when people chew loudly.

Pester — A specific type of annoying. To pester means to annoy someone by repeatedly asking for something or following them around.

The children pestered their mother for ice cream all afternoon.

Nag — To annoy someone by repeatedly criticizing them or reminding them to do something.

He nagged her about finishing her homework every single evening.

Vex — A more formal and slightly stronger word than annoy. To vex someone means to cause them irritation and worry. Used more in formal writing or older texts.

Get on someone's nerves — A very common idiom that means the same thing as annoy.

His constant whistling gets on my nerves.
To please, delight, soothe, or comfort someone are the natural opposites — to give them a positive or calming feeling rather than an irritating one.

These are natural combinations you will hear frequently:

  • "It really annoys me that..." — used to express frustration about a situation
  • "Stop annoying me!" — a direct command to someone bothering you
  • "What annoys me is..." — used to explain a specific irritant
  • "I find it annoying when..." — a softer, more reflective way to express the same
  • "Don't annoy the animals" — a common warning in zoos or when near pets
  • "You're being really annoying right now" — using the adjective form to describe someone's current behaviour

"Annoy" almost always needs an object — there must be a person (or group) being annoyed. You annoy someone. You cannot simply say "He annoys" and stop there; it sounds incomplete. The exception is the adjective form: "He is annoying" or "That sound is annoying," which can stand alone.
Putting It All Together — A Mental Picture

Imagine you are trying to sleep. A mosquito keeps flying near your ear. It buzzes. You swat it. It comes back. It buzzes again. You are not devastated. You are not weeping. You are not in a blind rage. But you are bothered. You are impatient. You want it to stop.

That mosquito is annoying you.

Now replace the mosquito with a person tapping their pen in a quiet room, or a car alarm going off outside your window, or a colleague who interrupts you every five minutes — the feeling is the same. Mild, persistent, nagging discomfort that you wish would go away.

That is precisely what "annoy" means.
783: Annoyance describes a mild, uncomfortable feeling — a kind of low-level dissatisfaction or displeasure that arises when something bothers, disturbs, or irritates you. It is not intense anger or rage. Think of it as the feeling you get when a mosquito keeps buzzing near your ear, or when someone talks loudly on their phone in a quiet place. You are bothered. You are not furious. That middle ground is annoyance.

The noun "annoyance" carries two closely related but distinct meanings. Understanding both is essential.

Meaning 1: The feeling itself (the emotion)

Here, "annoyance" refers to the internal state — what you feel inside when something bothers you.

"He listened with growing annoyance as the meeting dragged on."
"She tried to hide her annoyance, but her expression gave her away."
"To my annoyance, the flight was delayed again."

In this sense, it is usually uncountable — you don't say "an annoyance" when you mean the emotion itself. You simply say "annoyance" or "a feeling of annoyance."

Meaning 2: The thing (or person) that causes the feeling

Here, "annoyance" refers to the source — the thing, situation, or person that is making you feel that way. In this use, it is countable, meaning it can take "an" before it and can be made plural.

"The constant noise from the construction was a real annoyance."
"Slow internet is one of the biggest annoyances of modern life."
"My little brother can be such an annoyance sometimes."

So the word can point both inward (your feeling) and outward (the cause of that feeling). Context always makes clear which meaning is intended.
Where Annoyance Sits on the Emotional Scale

It helps to understand annoyance by seeing where it fits among related emotions. Imagine a scale from mildest to strongest:

Minor irritation → Annoyance → Frustration → Anger → Fury/Rage

Annoyance sits toward the lighter end. It is more than a passing flicker of irritation, but far less intense than full anger. It does not overwhelm you. You can still function normally while feeling it. Often, it is also temporary — it tends to fade once the source of bother is removed.

Annoyances are usually small, repeated, or persistent disturbances — the kind that wear on you rather than shock you. Common examples include:

  • Someone interrupting you repeatedly while you're trying to concentrate
  • A dripping tap you can't fix
  • A colleague who is always late
  • An ad that plays before every video
  • Being asked the same question over and over

Notice that none of these are catastrophic. They are minor problems, but they are irritating precisely because they keep happening or because they are out of your control.

Learning how a word is actually used in phrases is just as important as knowing its definition. Here are the most common patterns with "annoyance":

  • To someone's annoyance — meaning: causing that person to feel annoyed.
    "To her annoyance, no one had bothered to read the report."
  • With annoyance — used to describe how someone spoke, looked, or acted.
    "He glanced at his phone with obvious annoyance."
  • A source of annoyance — something that repeatedly causes this feeling.
    "The broken printer has been a constant source of annoyance for weeks."
  • Feel / express / show annoyance — standard verb collocations.
    "She felt a wave of annoyance but said nothing."
    "He expressed his annoyance calmly but clearly."
  • Minor / major / constant / growing annoyance — adjectives commonly paired with the word.
    "The tiny grammatical errors were a minor annoyance."
    "The traffic noise was a constant annoyance."
How Annoyance Differs From Similar Words

Irritation — Very close in meaning to annoyance. If anything, irritation can feel slightly quicker and sharper — a sudden flash of being bothered — whereas annoyance can feel more settled and sustained. In practice, the two words are often used interchangeably.

Frustration — Stronger than annoyance. Frustration usually involves being blocked from achieving something you want. You feel frustrated when your efforts aren't working. Annoyance doesn't require that sense of being blocked.

Nuisance — This word focuses more on the thing or person causing the problem, just like the second meaning of annoyance. However, "nuisance" has a slightly more formal or legal flavour (e.g., a legal nuisance, a public nuisance), while annoyance is more everyday and personal.

Vexation — A more formal and old-fashioned word meaning strong annoyance or frustration. You would see it in older literature. In modern everyday speech, "annoyance" is far more natural.

Exasperation — Stronger than annoyance. It suggests you have reached the end of your patience. You feel exasperated after being annoyed for a long time and the problem still hasn't stopped.

"Annoyance" is a neutral, standard English word — not too formal, not too casual. You can use it comfortably in everyday conversation, in writing, in professional emails, or in academic contexts. It carries no strong positive or negative connotation beyond the meaning itself.

Annoyance is the noun for that familiar, low-level feeling of being bothered or irritated by something that is unpleasant, disruptive, or inconvenient — but not seriously harmful. It can refer to the feeling itself ("I felt annoyance") or to whatever is causing that feeling ("The noise was an annoyance"). It lives in the middle of the emotional scale — stronger than a passing flicker of irritation, but much milder than genuine anger. The things that cause annoyance are usually small and persistent, and the feeling itself is temporary but genuinely uncomfortable while it lasts.
784:
An annuity is a financial arrangement in which a person receives a series of regular payments — typically monthly, quarterly, or yearly — either for a fixed period of time or for the rest of their life. The payments come from a sum of money that was invested or paid upfront, usually to an insurance company or financial institution.
