Think of it this way: instead of receiving a large pile of cash all at once, you receive smaller, steady amounts trickling in over time. The word "annuity" refers both to the arrangement itself and to the stream of payments that flows from it.

A simple way to picture it: imagine you hand an insurance company $200,000 today, and in return they promise to pay you $1,200 every month for as long as you live. That monthly payment is your annuity.
The Two Phases of an Annuity

Most annuities have two distinct phases:

The Accumulation Phase is when money goes in. You (or your employer, or someone on your behalf) deposit money — either as a single large payment or as a series of contributions over time. This money sits and grows, often earning interest or investment returns.

The Distribution Phase (also called the payout phase) is when money comes out. You start receiving your regular payments. This is the phase most people picture when they think of an annuity.

Not all annuities work the same way. They differ in three key dimensions:

By when payments start:

An immediate annuity begins paying you almost right away — typically within a month of your lump-sum deposit. You hand over your money, and payments start very soon. This is common for someone who is already retired and needs income right now.

A deferred annuity delays payments to a future date. You might pay into it for twenty years while you are still working, and only begin receiving payments when you retire. During the waiting period, your money accumulates and grows.

By how much you receive:

A fixed annuity pays you the exact same amount every period, no matter what. If it says $1,200 a month, you get $1,200 a month, always. This is predictable and safe, but it does not grow with inflation.

A variable annuity ties your payments to the performance of investments (like stocks or bonds). If your investments do well, you receive more. If they do poorly, you receive less. There is more potential reward but also more risk.

An indexed annuity (sometimes called an equity-indexed annuity) is a middle ground. Your returns are tied to a market index, like the S&P 500, but there is usually a floor (a minimum you cannot go below) and a cap (a maximum you can earn). It offers more growth potential than a fixed annuity but more protection than a variable one.

By how long payments last:

A life annuity pays you for as long as you are alive — even if you live to 110. You can never outlive it. However, if you die early, the payments simply stop and your heirs typically receive nothing remaining.

A fixed-period annuity (also called a term annuity) pays for a specific number of years — say, 10 or 20 years — regardless of whether you are alive or not. If you die before the period ends, your beneficiary continues receiving the payments.

A life with period certain annuity combines both: it pays for life, but guarantees a minimum number of years. If you die in year 3 of a "life with 10-year certain" annuity, your beneficiary gets payments for the remaining 7 years.

For couples, there is the joint and survivor annuity, which covers two people — typically spouses. Payments continue as long as either person is alive.

The primary reason is to guarantee income — especially in retirement. One of the biggest financial fears people have is outliving their money. A life annuity eliminates that fear entirely. No matter how long you live, the payments keep coming.

Annuities are also used to:

Turn a large windfall into manageable income. Lottery winners, for example, are often given the choice between a single lump sum or an annuity — annual payments spread over 20 or 30 years. The annuity option often has a higher total payout on paper, but the lump sum is more money in hand today.

Provide tax advantages. In many countries, the money inside a deferred annuity grows tax-deferred, meaning you do not pay taxes on the gains until you actually start withdrawing. This can allow your money to compound more efficiently over time.

Replace a salary. Businesses sometimes purchase annuities to fund pension obligations — promising retired employees a steady monthly income for life.

Many people interact with annuity-like arrangements without realizing it:

Social Security payments (in the United States) function like a life annuity. You pay into the system throughout your working life, and once you reach retirement age, you receive monthly payments for the rest of your life.

Pensions work the same way. An employer promises a retired worker a fixed monthly income for life — that is an annuity.

Structured settlements in legal cases sometimes pay out as annuities rather than a lump sum — the injured party receives a fixed monthly payment for years.
The Annuity Concept in Mathematics and Finance

In mathematics and finance, "annuity" has a slightly broader, more technical meaning. It refers to any series of equal payments made at regular intervals, regardless of context. This includes things like mortgage payments, car loan installments, bond coupon payments, or lease payments — all of these can be analyzed as annuities.

Financiers use the concept to calculate two important things:

The present value of an annuity — how much a future stream of payments is worth in today's money. For example, if someone promises to pay you $1,000 per year for 10 years, what is that stream of payments worth right now, given that money received in the future is worth less than money in hand today?

The future value of an annuity — how much a series of regular contributions will grow to by some point in the future. For example, if you save $500 per month for 30 years and earn 6% annual interest, how large will your account be?

These calculations underpin mortgages, retirement planning, insurance pricing, and bond valuation, among many other things.

Annuities are powerful tools but come with genuine downsides worth understanding:

Loss of liquidity. When you hand over a lump sum to purchase an annuity, you typically lose access to that capital. You cannot suddenly say "I need $50,000" and withdraw it. Your money is locked in, converted into a payment stream.

Mortality risk. With a life annuity, you are essentially making a bet on how long you will live. If you die young, you may receive far less than you paid in, and your heirs get nothing. The insurance company keeps the remainder. On the other hand, if you live to a very old age, you could receive far more than you originally paid — which is the whole point.

Inflation risk. A fixed annuity paying $1,200 a month sounds good today, but in 20 years, inflation may have eroded that purchasing power significantly. $1,200 in 20 years might feel like $800 feels today. Variable and indexed annuities address this somewhat, but fixed annuities do not.

Fees. Variable annuities in particular can carry high fees — administrative fees, mortality and expense charges, fund management fees — which eat into your returns.

Counterparty risk. Your payments depend on the financial health of the institution backing the annuity. If that institution collapses, your payments could be at risk (though most countries have regulatory protections in place to limit this).
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

You might encounter "annuity" in several different contexts:

In everyday personal finance: "She used her retirement savings to purchase an annuity that pays her $2,000 a month for life."

In legal documents or wills: "The estate shall provide an annuity of $10,000 per year to the deceased's surviving spouse."

In mathematics or business: "Calculate the present value of a 20-year annuity paying $5,000 annually at a discount rate of 5%."

In journalism or news: "The lottery winner chose the annuity option, which pays out over 26 years instead of a single lump sum."

An annuity is a promise of steady, repeated payments over time — either in exchange for a lump sum invested earlier, or as the result of ongoing contributions. It converts wealth into income. It is the financial world's answer to a simple human need: the certainty of knowing that money will keep arriving, regularly and reliably, no matter what. Whether you encounter the word in a retirement brochure, a math textbook, a legal document, or a news article, that core idea — a stream of regular payments — is always at its center.
785:
To annul something means to officially and completely wipe it out — not just stop it, but declare that it has no legal force whatsoever, often treating it as though it never existed in the first place.

Think of it like an eraser on a legal document. You're not crossing something out — you're erasing it entirely, so that in the eyes of the law, there's nothing left.

The word is almost always used in a formal or legal setting. Ordinary people don't "annul" their lunch plans. Courts, governments, churches, and official institutions annul things. That formality is baked into the word itself.

The second thing that makes annul powerful is its retroactive quality. Many words describe ending something going forward. Annul often goes a step further — it says the thing was invalid from the very beginning. It doesn't just say "this is over." It says "this never had any legal standing to begin with."

1. Marriage
This is by far the most common context. When a marriage is annulled, it means a court or church has declared that the marriage was never legally or validly formed. The result is different from a divorce. A divorce ends a marriage that was real and valid. An annulment says: there was no real marriage at all. The couple is treated, in legal terms, as though they were never married.

2. Contracts and Agreements
A contract can be annulled if it was formed under fraud, coercion, or some other flaw that made it invalid from the start. When annulled, the contract carries no obligations — it's as if it was never signed.

3. Laws and Official Decisions
A court can annul a law passed by a government body, declaring it to have no legal effect. Similarly, official decisions — like an election result or a ruling — can be annulled if found to be illegal or improperly made.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are easy to confuse with annul, so it helps to line them up:

Annul vs. Cancel
Cancel simply ends something — it stops it from continuing or happening. Annul goes further and wipes out its legal existence entirely, often retroactively. You cancel a subscription. You annul a marriage.

Annul vs. Revoke
Revoke takes something back from this moment forward — like revoking a driving licence. The thing existed and was valid up until the moment it was revoked. Annul is stronger — it questions the validity of the thing even from its origin.

Annul vs. Nullify
These two are the closest pair. Both mean to render something void. Nullify is slightly broader and can be used more loosely in everyday language. Annul is the more formal, legally precise term, and is especially preferred when talking about marriages, contracts, and legal acts.

Annul vs. Repeal
Repeal is used almost exclusively for laws and legislation. A government repeals a law. Annul can apply to a wider range of things — marriages, contracts, decisions — and carries that retroactive force that repeal does not always imply.

Annul vs. Void (verb)
To void something means to make it invalid. It's very similar to annul in result. However, annul is the more formal and official action — the act of an authority declaring something void. Void simply describes the outcome or state; annul describes the authoritative act.

Annul is a strong and final word. When something is annulled, there is no partial undoing — it is completely stripped of its legal force. It carries weight precisely because it is not used casually. Its use signals that an authority has made a definitive, official declaration.
Quick Examples to Lock It In

• The court annulled the contract because one party had signed it under threats.
  • The bishop annulled the marriage after determining it had never been valid.
  • The election results were annulled due to widespread fraud.
  • The judge annulled the earlier ruling, declaring it to have been unlawful from the start.
To annul is to officially and formally declare something — usually a marriage, contract, law, or decision — to be legally void and without effect, often as though it had never validly existed at all.
786:
An annulment is an official declaration — made by a court, a legal authority, or a religious institution — that something never validly existed in the first place. It doesn't just end something; it wipes it out retroactively, as though it was never real or legitimate from the very beginning.

Think of it this way: if you draw a line on paper and then erase it, the line is gone. That's closer to annulment. If you simply cross it out, that's closer to cancellation or divorce. Annulment says: "This line was never supposed to be here."

Annulment is used in a few important contexts.

1. Marriage (the most common use)

This is where most people encounter the word. A marriage annulment is a legal or religious ruling that a marriage was invalid — not just broken, but fundamentally flawed from the start, as if the wedding never legally happened.

This is very different from a divorce. A divorce says: "We had a real, valid marriage, and now we are ending it." An annulment says: "This marriage was never legally valid to begin with."

Because of this distinction, after an annulment, both people are legally treated as though they were never married to each other at all.

But when is a marriage considered invalid from the start? Courts in most countries will grant a marriage annulment only under specific grounds, such as:

  • Fraud or deception — One person lied about something fundamental, such as hiding a serious illness, concealing an addiction, or lying about being able to have children when that was agreed upon.
  • Bigamy — One of the people was already legally married to someone else at the time of the wedding, making the second marriage automatically void.
  • Being underage — One or both people were below the legal age to marry and did not have required parental or court approval.
  • Lack of mental capacity — One person was not mentally capable of understanding what marriage means — for example, due to severe mental illness or being under the heavy influence of alcohol or drugs at the time of the ceremony.
  • Duress — One person was forced or threatened into the marriage against their will. A freely given consent is essential for a valid marriage; without it, there is no real marriage.
  • Close blood relation — Marriage between people who are close relatives (like siblings or first cousins, depending on the law of the place) is legally forbidden and therefore void.
  • Inability to consummate — In some legal systems, if a marriage was never physically consummated, and one spouse was permanently unable to do so (and hid this fact), it can be grounds for annulment.

An important note about children: Even when a marriage is annulled, children born during that marriage are not considered illegitimate. The law protects children from the consequences of their parents' invalid marriage. The children's legal rights — such as inheritance rights — remain intact.

2. Contracts and Legal Agreements

Annulment also applies to contracts. A contract can be annulled if it was made under fraud, threats, or by someone who legally lacked the capacity to enter into it (for example, a minor or someone with a severe cognitive disability). Once annulled, the contract is treated as though it never existed, and both parties are returned — as far as possible — to the position they were in before signing it.

3. Decisions, Elections, and Laws

Courts and authorities can annul decisions, elections, or laws that were conducted or passed improperly. For example, if an election is found to have been carried out with serious fraud, it may be annulled — meaning it is struck from the record and treated as though it never validly took place.

4. Religious Annulment

Religious institutions — most notably the Catholic Church — also issue annulments, but these are entirely separate from legal/civil annulments. A Church annulment (formally called a "declaration of nullity") is the Church's ruling that, despite appearances, a valid sacramental marriage (a marriage recognized by the Church as a true, sacred bond) never actually came into existence. This might be because one or both partners lacked genuine commitment, were secretly intending not to honor their vows, or were psychologically incapable of fulfilling the duties of marriage.

This does not automatically affect your legal marital status in your country — it is a purely religious ruling within the Church. Similarly, a civil/legal annulment has no effect on your standing within a religious institution.

If there is one idea to anchor in your mind, it is this:

Annulment ≠ ending something. Annulment = declaring that something was never legitimately real.

Divorce ends a marriage. Annulment erases one. Terminating a contract ends it going forward. Annulling a contract treats it as though it was never binding. This retroactive quality — the reaching back in time to declare invalidity — is what separates annulment from every other form of ending or cancellation.

What it isAn official ruling that something was invalid from the very start
What it is NOTA way of simply ending or canceling something
Most common useMarriage
The key ideaIt looks backward and says "this was never valid", not forward and says "this is now over"

"The court granted an annulment of the marriage on the grounds that the groom had already been legally married to another person."
787:
When something is described as anodyne, it means it is so carefully designed to be safe, inoffensive, and unlikely to upset anyone that it ends up being dull, empty, or meaningless. It is the word you reach for when something has been so thoroughly drained of anything bold, sharp, or controversial that it has lost its substance entirely.

Think of it this way: imagine a politician is asked a hard question. Instead of answering it honestly — which might upset some people — they give a vague, pleasant-sounding non-answer that says nothing at all. That response is anodyne. It caused zero offence, but also conveyed zero meaning. That trade-off — safety in exchange for substance — is exactly what the word captures.

This is critical to using the word correctly: anodyne almost always carries a mildly critical or disapproving tone. You are not simply saying something is harmless. You are saying that in its effort to be harmless, it became hollow. The word quietly signals that something should have had more substance, more courage, or more real content — but it was deliberately softened until nothing worthwhile remained.

So when a writer calls a speech, a report, or a book "anodyne," they are not complimenting its peacefulness. They are criticising its emptiness.

There is a secondary meaning of anodyne that is softer and less critical: soothing, or relieving pain and distress. In this sense, anodyne describes something that gently calms or eases discomfort — emotionally or otherwise. This meaning is less common in everyday modern writing, but you will encounter it in literary or formal contexts.

For example, someone might offer anodyne words of reassurance to a grieving friend — words that are gentle and comforting, even if they can't truly fix the situation.

These two meanings are connected by a shared thread: mildness. Whether something is anodyne because it avoids controversy or because it soothes pain, the quality in both cases is one of deliberate gentleness — of having all the sharp edges removed.

Here are examples across both meanings so you can see the word in action:

In the critical sense (most common):

  • "The committee released an anodyne statement that acknowledged the problem but committed to nothing." — The statement was so vague and safe that it was essentially meaningless.
  • "His novels started out bold and provocative, but his later work became increasingly anodyne — written, it seemed, to offend no one and therefore to say nothing."
  • "The pop star's new album is frustratingly anodyne: catchy, clean, and completely forgettable."

In the soothing sense:

  • "She found his presence strangely anodyne — his calm voice and unhurried manner made her anxiety loosen its grip."
  • "The therapist offered a few anodyne observations at first, simply helping the patient feel heard before going deeper."
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

Several words overlap with anodyne, but none of them mean exactly the same thing.

Bland means lacking strong flavour or character — it describes something dull, but without necessarily implying that someone worked to make it that way. Anodyne, on the other hand, implies that the dullness is often deliberate — the result of caution, political calculation, or a desire to avoid offending anyone.

Harmless is neutral and even positive — it simply means something will not hurt you. Anodyne goes further: yes, it won't hurt you, but it won't do much of anything else either.

Inoffensive is the closest near-synonym in the critical sense, but it lacks the disapproving edge that anodyne carries. Calling something inoffensive is a mild shrug. Calling it anodyne is a quiet but pointed criticism.

Soothing overlaps with the second meaning, but soothing is purely positive. Anodyne in this sense has a slightly more clinical or restrained quality — it calms, but perhaps without warmth.
Who Uses This Word and Where

Anodyne is a formal or literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in:

  • Journalism and political commentary ("an anodyne press release," "anodyne campaign promises")
  • Literary or film criticism ("an anodyne screenplay that never takes risks")
  • Formal essays or academic writing

You would rarely hear it in casual conversation. If someone used it in everyday speech, it would sound deliberately sophisticated or slightly old-fashioned.

If you forget everything else, hold onto this: anodyne = so carefully inoffensive that it becomes meaningless. It is the word for something that has been sanded down until all the edges are gone — safe to touch, but no longer shaped like anything in particular.
788:
To anoint someone means to deliberately apply oil — or sometimes another liquid — to a person's body, usually as a meaningful, ceremonial act. But the word almost never stops at just the physical action. Anointing is almost always done for a reason: to bless, consecrate, honor, or mark someone as specially chosen.

This is the key insight: if you pour cooking oil into a frying pan, you don't anoint it. But if a priest pours sacred oil on a person's head during a religious ceremony, that is anointing. The difference is purpose and significance. Anointing is never casual — it always carries weight.

1. The Literal, Ceremonial Meaning

This is the original and oldest use of the word. Anointing with oil is one of humanity's most ancient rituals, practiced across many religions and cultures. In this sense, to anoint someone means to apply oil to them as a sacred act — to bless them, purify them, or officially mark them as set apart for a holy or important purpose.

People have been anointed for many reasons throughout history:

  • To install them as a king, priest, or leader (the oil symbolizes divine blessing and authority)
  • To consecrate them — meaning to make them sacred or dedicated to God
  • To heal them — in many religious traditions, anointing the sick is an act of prayer and care
  • To prepare a body for burial (this appears in ancient texts including the Bible)

Examples in sentences:

  • "The high priest anointed the new king with oil, marking the beginning of his reign."
  • "During the ceremony, the bishop anointed the young man's hands as he became a priest."
  • "The women came to anoint Jesus's body after the crucifixion."

One fact that shows you how central this concept is to religion: the word Messiah in Hebrew and Christ in Greek both literally mean "the anointed one" — a person who has been chosen and set apart by God. That tells you everything about the spiritual weight this word carries.

2. The Figurative Meaning — To Officially Choose or Declare Someone

Over time, "anoint" moved beyond religion into everyday language. Today, it is very commonly used figuratively to mean: to officially select, declare, or endorse someone as especially important — typically as a future leader, successor, or top choice — usually because someone powerful or influential is doing the choosing.

In this figurative use, no oil is involved at all. It's purely about the idea of elevation and selection.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The retiring CEO anointed her deputy as the company's next leader."
  • "The senior politicians anointed him as their preferred candidate long before the election."
  • "By giving him the most prestigious project, the director essentially anointed him as the team's rising star."

Notice the common thread: in every example, someone with authority is choosing someone else and lifting them up. This is crucial — anointing is not something you do to yourself. It comes from above. A king doesn't anoint himself; a priest, a prophet, or a powerful figure does it. Similarly, in the figurative sense, you don't anoint yourself as a leader — others do it for you.

3. A General, Non-Religious Literal Use

Occasionally, "anoint" is used simply to mean to apply oil or liquid to someone's body, with no religious meaning at all.

  • "She anointed her skin with warm coconut oil."
  • "The healer anointed the wound with herbal oil."

This use is less common in everyday conversation — most people would just say "rubbed" or "applied." Using "anoint" here sounds elevated, old-fashioned, or literary. But you will encounter it, especially in older texts.
The Feeling the Word Always Carries

Across all its uses, "anoint" consistently carries one feeling: being set apart from the ordinary. An anointed person is not just assigned a role — they are elevated, chosen, blessed. There is almost always a sense of ceremony, destiny, or special status attached to the word. This is what separates it from plainer words like "choose," "appoint," or "select."
How to Use It in a Sentence

Anoint almost always follows this structure:

[Someone] anoints [someone] [with something] [as something]

  • "The priest anointed the child with holy oil." (with = the substance used)
  • "The board anointed her as the next chairperson." (as = the role she is elevated to)
  • "He was anointed the heir by the outgoing leader."

Anointed (adjective or past tense verb): Describes someone who has been anointed.

  • "She is the anointed successor."
  • "The king was anointed at dawn."

Anointing (noun or present participle): The act of applying oil or the broader act of choosing.

  • "The anointing of the sick is a holy sacrament in Catholicism."
  • "His anointing as the next leader surprised many."

Anointment (noun): The result or act of anointing.

  • "Her anointment as champion was celebrated by her supporters."

The Anointed One (phrase): A title for someone divinely chosen — most famously used to refer to the Messiah or Christ.

Self-anointed (adjective): This is a critically used phrase. It describes someone who declares themselves to be special, important, or an authority — without being genuinely chosen or recognized by others. It is almost always used to mock or dismiss someone.

  • "He is a self-anointed expert with no real credentials."
  • "She is the self-anointed voice of the people."
Anoint vs. Appoint — Don't Confuse Them

These two words sound similar and both involve placing someone in a role, but they feel very different.

Appoint is practical and neutral. It simply means to officially give someone a job or role.

  • "She was appointed as the new head of the department." — No ceremony, no grand significance. Just an assignment.

Anoint is grander, more ceremonial, and implies a sense of being "the chosen one."

  • "She was anointed as the future of the company." — This suggests she's been singled out as exceptional, blessed by those in power, destined for greatness.

If your manager emails you saying you got a promotion, that's an appointment.
If your manager publicly declares you to be the future star of the organization and everyone starts treating you differently, that's closer to anointment.

To anoint someone means to apply oil to them — usually as part of a religious ceremony — in order to bless them, consecrate them, or officially mark them as chosen for an important role. By extension, it means to officially select or endorse someone as special or as a future leader, without any literal oil involved. The word always carries a sense of elevation, ceremony, and being set apart from the ordinary. It implies that someone with authority has deliberately lifted another person up and marked them as significant. The opposite of this feeling would be something bland and bureaucratic — anointing is always meaningful, always carries weight, and always suggests that the person receiving it is no longer ordinary.
789:
Anointing is the act of deliberately applying oil — or sometimes another substance — to a person or object as a meaningful, intentional gesture. The word always implies that this is not just a casual, accidental, or practical act. It is purposeful. It carries weight. It communicates something.

Think of it as a physical act that carries a spiritual or symbolic message.

In its most literal sense, an anointing involves pouring, dripping, or rubbing oil onto someone — usually on the head or forehead, though sometimes the entire body or specific body parts depending on the context. The oil used is typically special — olive oil is the most traditional — and in religious settings, it is often mixed with fragrances and formally blessed beforehand, making it what is called "holy oil" or "sacred oil."

The physical act itself is almost always simple and brief. A person anoints another by placing oil on their skin with a deliberate, ritualistic intention.
Why Oil? The Symbolism Behind It

To understand anointing fully, you need to understand why oil was chosen as the medium in the first place.

In ancient cultures, oil was precious. It was used to keep skin soft and healthy, to make hair gleam, to fuel lamps that gave light in darkness, and to preserve and protect things from decay. Because of these qualities, oil became a powerful symbol:

  • Light and clarity — it fuels lamps
  • Life and health — it nourishes skin and body
  • Protection — it preserves against deterioration
  • Honor and celebration — being oiled was a sign that you were valued, prepared, and set apart

When religious traditions adopted oil for their rituals, they brought all of this symbolism along with it. To anoint someone meant, symbolically, to prepare them, protect them, honor them, and set them apart for a special purpose.
The Religious Meaning — The Heart of the Word

This is where anointing becomes truly rich and important. Across several major religions — especially within Judaism and Christianity — an anointing is not simply a nice gesture. It is a deeply sacred act with layers of meaning.

1. Being Set Apart (Consecration)

An anointing marks a person or object as holy — meaning "set apart for God's purposes." When a priest, a king, a prophet, or a place of worship is anointed, the act is a declaration: This person or this thing no longer belongs to the ordinary world. They now belong to God and to His purposes.

This is why objects like altars, temples, and sacred vessels were also anointed in the Hebrew Bible. It was a way of formally dedicating them to divine use.

2. Divine Selection and Authority

In the ancient world of the Bible, kings were not simply crowned — they were anointed. This was enormously significant. It meant their authority did not come from their own power or from popular vote. It came from God. The anointing was the moment God's choice was made visible and official.

When the prophet Samuel anointed David with oil, it was not merely a ceremony. It was the declaration that God had personally selected David to lead His people. The oil was the tangible, physical sign of that divine appointment.

3. The Presence and Power of the Holy Spirit

In Christian theology, an anointing is closely associated with the Holy Spirit — God's own spirit — coming upon a person. The oil is a symbol of the Spirit. To be anointed, therefore, is understood as being filled with or empowered by the Spirit of God for a specific task or calling.

This is why, in Charismatic and Pentecostal Christian communities especially, people speak of "the anointing" as a present, felt spiritual power. A preacher might be described as having "a strong anointing" — meaning that when they speak, there is a sense of divine energy, authority, and effectiveness flowing through them that goes beyond mere human skill or preparation.

4. Healing

Anointing is also strongly associated with healing. In the New Testament, the disciples of Jesus anointed sick people with oil as part of praying for their recovery. The Epistle of James explicitly instructs church elders to anoint the sick with oil and pray over them. In Catholic, Orthodox, and some Protestant traditions, this remains a living practice. The Catholic sacrament known as the Anointing of the Sick (historically called Last Rites or Extreme Unction) is given to people who are gravely ill or close to death — not only to pray for physical healing, but also to bring spiritual comfort, forgiveness of sins, and preparation for the possibility of death.

5. Ordination and Commission

When someone is being installed into a formal religious role — a priest, a bishop, sometimes a deacon — an anointing can be part of the ceremony. It is a physical act that says: You are now officially set apart, empowered, and commissioned for this sacred work.

6. The Word "Messiah" and "Christ"

Here is one of the most important facts about this word: The term Messiah (from Hebrew) means literally the Anointed One. The term Christ (from Greek) means exactly the same thing — the Anointed One.

So when Christians call Jesus "Christ," they are calling him the one who has been anointed by God — the one supremely chosen, set apart, empowered, and commissioned for the most important mission in history. This single fact shows just how central anointing is to the entire Judeo-Christian tradition.

Because anointing has carried such strong associations with selection, appointment, and the conferring of special status, the word has moved into everyday secular language with a related meaning.

When someone says, "The outgoing CEO has anointed his successor," they do not mean there was actual oil involved. They mean: the current leader has personally chosen, endorsed, and designated a specific person as the next leader — often in a way that carries weight and is not easily questioned.

In this usage, an anointing implies:

  • That someone in authority has made a deliberate choice
  • That the chosen person is being elevated above others
  • That a kind of unofficial but powerful approval has been bestowed

You might also hear it in sports, politics, or entertainment: "She was anointed as the next great star of her generation" — meaning she was singled out and elevated as the obvious, destined successor to greatness.

The tone can sometimes be slightly skeptical or critical in this secular use — implying that someone was hand-picked by insiders rather than earning their position through open competition.

No matter the context, an anointing always carries one or more of these ideas:

  • Selection — this person has been specifically chosen
  • Authorization — they now carry real authority, often divine in origin
  • Empowerment — they have been given something beyond themselves to accomplish their task
  • Consecration — they are set apart from the ordinary
  • Blessing — they have received favor and goodwill, often from above
  • Transition — they are crossing a threshold from one state or role into another
A Concrete Example to Tie It Together

Imagine a new king is about to take the throne. There is a ceremony. A religious leader steps forward, takes a small horn or vessel of holy oil, and pours it over the king's head. That act — that anointing — is the moment everything changes. It is not the crown on his head or the cheering of the crowd that makes him king in the deepest sense. It is the oil. Because the oil says: God has chosen this man. God is with him. God is empowering him. His rule is not just a political fact — it is a sacred one.

That is the full weight of an anointing.
790:
Anointment means the act of anointing — that is, the act of applying oil or a sacred liquid to a person (or sometimes an object) as part of a ceremony. But beyond the physical act of applying oil, anointment carries a much deeper meaning: it is a formal act that sets someone apart as specially chosen, blessed, or elevated above others.

Think of it this way: when you anoint someone, you are not just putting oil on them. You are marking them as someone special — someone selected for an important role, someone who now carries a kind of divine or official blessing.

1. The Literal, Ceremonial Meaning

In its most traditional sense, anointment refers to a religious or royal ceremony in which oil is applied to a person's head, hands, or body. This has been practiced for thousands of years across many cultures and religions.

In religion:

  • In Christianity, anointment is a sacred act performed by a priest or religious leader. It is used in rituals like the anointing of the sick (when a seriously ill person is blessed before death), baptism, and the ordination of priests.
  • In the Bible's Old Testament, kings and prophets were anointed with oil to signify that God had chosen them and given them authority. In fact, the word Messiah in Hebrew and Christ in Greek both literally mean "the anointed one" — a title given to someone whom God has specially chosen.
  • In Hinduism and several other traditions, anointing with oil or ghee (clarified butter) is part of various religious ceremonies too.

In royal coronations:

  • When a king or queen is crowned, one of the most sacred and central parts of the ceremony is their anointment. A religious leader pours or applies holy oil onto the monarch's head, hands, or chest. This act symbolizes that the ruler has received divine approval and blessing to govern.
  • This is not an ancient, dead tradition — King Charles III of the United Kingdom, for example, was anointed during his coronation in 2023, making it one of the most spiritually significant moments of the ceremony.

The key idea in all these literal uses: anointment marks a moment of divine or official blessing, and the person anointed is recognized as specially chosen or consecrated.

2. The Figurative Meaning (Everyday Modern Use)

Over time, the word anointment moved beyond religious and royal settings and entered everyday language with a broader, figurative meaning.

Today, when people use "anointment" outside a religious context, they mean:

The act of officially or informally choosing and designating someone as the successor, leader, or favored person for an important role.

This figurative use borrows the spirit of the original meaning — just as a king was anointed to signal "this is the chosen one," we now use anointment to describe situations where a powerful person or institution picks someone out and signals to the world that this is the person they have selected.

Examples of this figurative use:

  • "The retiring CEO's anointment of her deputy as successor came as a surprise to the board." (The CEO informally but clearly chose and designated her deputy as the next leader.)
  • "His anointment as the party's presidential candidate was made official at the national convention." (He was formally selected and declared the chosen candidate.)
  • "Many felt that the director's anointment of his own son as the next head of the studio was an act of nepotism." (He chose his son and elevated him to the position.)

Notice that in all these cases, no oil is involved — the word is being used metaphorically. But the feeling it carries is the same: someone is being specially selected and elevated, often by a person or group with authority.

Anointment is not a neutral word. It carries certain connotations (feelings and associations) that are important to understand:

  • Elevation: The anointed person is being lifted above others. They are not just selected from a list — they are set apart as special.
  • Authority and legitimacy: Anointment implies that the selection comes from someone with power or authority (God, a king, a CEO, a political party). It gives the chosen person a sense of legitimacy.
  • Solemnity: Whether used literally or figuratively, anointment has a serious, weighty tone. It is not a casual choice — it feels deliberate and significant.
  • Sometimes, criticism: In modern political or business language, "anointment" can carry a slightly negative or skeptical tone. When journalists write that a leader "anointed" their successor, they sometimes imply that the choice was made undemocratically — without consulting others, as if by royal decree. It can suggest that the chosen person received preferential treatment rather than earning the position through fair competition.
Common Contexts Where You'll See This Word

ContextWhat it refers to

You will encounter "anointment" most frequently in these areas:

  • Religious writing and scripture — referring to sacred rituals of blessing
  • Coverage of royal events — especially coronation ceremonies
  • Political journalism — when a party, faction, or powerful figure designates a preferred candidate or successor
  • Business reporting — when a senior leader openly designates the next person to lead an organization
  • Sports commentary — occasionally, when a young athlete is declared the "next great one" by coaches or the media ("his anointment as the heir to the throne of the sport")
A Few Example Sentences to Solidify Your Understanding

• "The priest performed the anointment of the dying man, offering prayers and applying sacred oil to his forehead."
  • "The anointment of King Solomon, as described in scripture, was a solemn ceremony that marked the beginning of his reign."
  • "Her anointment as the firm's managing partner came after fifteen years of dedicated work."
  • "Critics argued that the anointment of the chairman's nephew as director bypassed dozens of more qualified candidates."
  • "The young musician's anointment by the legendary producer opened every door in the industry for her."

Anointment is the act of applying sacred oil to a person as part of a ceremony (to bless, consecrate, or officially recognize them), or, in everyday figurative use, the act of choosing and designating someone as a specially selected person for an important role — always carrying a sense of elevation, authority, and deliberate selection.
791:
Anomalous means departing from what is normal, expected, or standard. If something is anomalous, it doesn't fit the established pattern that everything else around it follows. It stands out as an exception — something that isn't supposed to be there, or at least isn't typically there, based on what's usual.

Picture a row of white eggs in a carton, and one is bright blue. That blue egg is anomalous — it breaks the pattern. Or imagine a scientist measuring the temperature of a chemical reaction, and every single experiment gives a reading of around 50°C — but one day, without any change to the setup, the reading shoots to 200°C. That reading is anomalous. It doesn't fit what's expected.

The single most important idea to grasp here: there must be a norm or a pattern for something to be anomalous against. Without a baseline of what's "normal," nothing can be anomalous. The word always implies a contrast with an established expectation. This is what separates it from just being "strange" or "unusual" — anomalous is precise. It points to a specific, measurable departure from a specific standard.

Anomalous is largely a neutral word. It doesn't automatically mean something is bad, dangerous, or broken. It simply means it's out of the ordinary. Whether that's a good thing or a bad thing depends entirely on the context.

A patient who recovers from a disease far faster than all other patients shows an anomalous recovery — and that's wonderful. A bridge showing anomalous stress fractures is deeply alarming. An anomalous spike in a company's sales could be exciting news. The word describes the departure from the norm, not the quality of that departure. This neutrality is one of the reasons scientists and researchers love this word — it lets them flag something as unexpected without jumping to conclusions about what it means.

Anomalous appears across many fields, always carrying the same core idea but applied to different settings.

In science and data, anomalous is extremely common. Scientists use it to flag results, readings, or data points that don't match what their theory or prior experiments would predict. An anomalous reading might mean equipment malfunctioned, or — more excitingly — it might hint at a genuine discovery. Many great scientific breakthroughs began as anomalous results that refused to be ignored.

In everyday language, you might describe someone's behavior as anomalous when they act completely out of character. If a person who is usually cheerful and talkative is silent and withdrawn one day, that's anomalous behavior for them — it stands out against their established norm.

In weather and nature, anomalous describes conditions that break from historical patterns — an anomalous cold snap in summer, anomalous rainfall in a desert, or anomalous warmth in a region that's typically frozen.

In law and grammar, anomalous cases are ones that don't fit the standard rules cleanly — exceptions that the system doesn't have a neat, ready-made answer for.

It's easy to blur anomalous with similar-sounding ideas, so let's draw the lines clearly.

Rare means something doesn't happen often. Anomalous means it doesn't fit the pattern. Something can be rare but completely expected — a solar eclipse is rare, but astronomers can predict it centuries in advance. It's not anomalous at all. Conversely, something anomalous might actually appear quite frequently in a dataset; what makes it anomalous is that it doesn't match the pattern, not how often it shows up.

Strange or weird are informal words that express personal surprise. Anomalous is more precise and objective — it means something measurably departs from a defined standard, regardless of whether you personally find it surprising or not.

Wrong implies an error or a mistake. Anomalous doesn't carry that judgment. An anomalous result can be perfectly correct and accurately measured — it's just unexpected given the pattern. Calling something anomalous is describing it, not condemning it.
Close Synonyms — And How They Differ

Several words share territory with anomalous, but each one has its own shade of meaning.

Abnormal is the most common everyday alternative. It carries a slightly stronger negative or clinical tone. In medicine, you'd say test results are "abnormal." A scientist, wanting to stay neutral and precise, would prefer "anomalous." Abnormal often implies that something should be fixed or is a cause for concern; anomalous is more detached.

Atypical means "not typical of its type or category." It's gentler and softer than abnormal. An atypical response to a drug is one that most patients don't experience. It focuses on category membership rather than deviation from a measured baseline.

Irregular focuses on a lack of pattern, rhythm, or consistency. An irregular heartbeat, irregular payments. It's more about predictability and repetition than about expectation.

Aberrant is stronger and often carries a negative moral edge. It suggests straying from the correct or socially accepted path — aberrant behavior in people tends to imply something more than just statistically unexpected; it implies something problematic or deviant.

Anomalous sits as the most precise and scientific of these. More neutral than "aberrant" or "abnormal," more tied to a specific baseline than "atypical," and broader in scope than "irregular."

The direct opposites of anomalous are words like: normal, typical, standard, expected, regular, consistent, and usual. Something is the antonym of anomalous when it fits perfectly within the expected pattern — when it's exactly what you'd predict, no surprises.

Anomalous naturally pairs with certain words, and knowing these will help you recognise it in the wild and use it confidently yourself.

You'll hear and read: anomalous results, anomalous findings, anomalous readings, anomalous data (all from scientific or analytical contexts); anomalous behavior (describing people, animals, or systems); anomalous conditions or anomalous weather (describing nature); anomalous situation or anomalous case (in legal, logical, or everyday contexts); and anomalous position (when something or someone occupies an unusual or hard-to-categorise standing).

Anomalous is a formal word. You'll encounter it most in academic writing, scientific papers, professional reports, technical documentation, and quality journalism. In casual conversation, people almost always reach for simpler words: weird, odd, unusual, out of place, or out of the ordinary.

Using anomalous in conversation isn't wrong at all — it just signals precision. It's especially powerful when you want to convey that you're comparing something against a specific, defined standard rather than just expressing personal surprise or confusion.

If something is anomalous, it:

departs from an established norm, pattern, or expectation; is measurably out of place relative to a known baseline; is described in a neutral, precise, and formal way; and does not automatically mean bad, wrong, or broken — only unexpected.

The next time you see a data point that sticks out from the rest, a person who acts in a way completely unlike themselves, or a situation that simply doesn't fit what logic or history would predict — that's your cue. The word is anomalous.
792:
An anomaly is something that does not fit the normal pattern. It is a thing, event, person, or situation that stands out because it is different from what is expected or usual in its surroundings.

Think of it this way: if you line up 100 red apples and one of them is blue, that blue apple is an anomaly. Everything else follows the expected pattern. That one thing does not. That is the heart of the word.

The key to truly understanding "anomaly" is understanding that it is always relative. Something can only be an anomaly in comparison to something else — a rule, a pattern, a standard, or a norm. Without a "normal," there can be no anomaly.

So there are always two sides to an anomaly:

The norm — what is regular, expected, or standard.
The anomaly — the one thing that breaks away from that norm.

An anomaly is not just something rare. It is something that actively contradicts or deviates from an established pattern. Rarity alone does not make something an anomaly — it must genuinely not belong to the pattern.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

The word "anomaly" is used across many different fields and everyday life. Here is how it appears in different contexts:

In science and data, an anomaly is a data point or result that does not match the trend. If a scientist is measuring the temperature of a lake every day for a year and one reading is suddenly 40 degrees higher than all the others, that reading is an anomaly. It signals that something unusual happened — maybe a malfunction, maybe a real event worth investigating.

In medicine, an anomaly refers to an irregularity in the body — something that differs from how the body normally looks or functions. A doctor might discover a structural anomaly in the heart, meaning the heart is shaped or built differently from the typical human heart.

In weather, a temperature anomaly means the temperature is significantly higher or lower than the historical average for that time and place. Climate scientists frequently use this term.

In everyday life, you might call a person an anomaly if they defy all typical expectations — for example, someone who never seems to get tired no matter how much work they do, in a world where everyone else gets exhausted. They are an anomaly among people.

In technology and computing, an anomaly is an unexpected behavior in a system. If a computer program suddenly acts differently from how it always has, with no apparent reason, that strange behavior is called an anomaly.

"Anomaly" is a neutral word on its own — it does not judge whether the unusual thing is good or bad. A medical anomaly could be harmless or dangerous. A statistical anomaly in a business could mean a surprisingly great month or a terrible one. The word simply signals: this does not fit.

However, in most practical situations, anomalies tend to attract attention and demand explanation, because humans and systems are built around patterns. When something breaks a pattern, the natural instinct is to ask: why?

The singular form is anomaly (one unusual thing).
The plural form is anomalies (multiple unusual things).

Example: "The test showed one anomaly in the data."
Example: "The scientist noticed several anomalies in the results."

These words share ground with "anomaly" but are not identical:

Irregularity — a broader term for anything that breaks a rule or pattern, but it often feels more minor and administrative. An anomaly tends to feel more significant and surprising.

Exception — something that is excluded from a rule or does not follow it, but an exception can be planned or expected. An anomaly is almost always unexpected.

Outlier — used mainly in statistics and data. An outlier is a data point far from the rest. While similar, "outlier" is more technical and narrower. An anomaly can be used more broadly.

Aberration — very close in meaning to anomaly, but "aberration" often carries a slight negative tone and implies something has gone wrong or deviated in an undesirable way.
A Few Natural Examples in Sentences

• "The warm winter was an anomaly — it had not happened in over a century."
  • "Doctors discovered a small anomaly in his scan, but assured him it was harmless."
  • "She was an anomaly in her field: entirely self-taught, yet more skilled than most professionals."
  • "The sudden drop in sales was an anomaly that the company could not immediately explain."
  • "Every experiment showed the same result, except one — that single test remained an anomaly."
An anomaly is anything that stands out because it breaks the expected pattern — it is the thing that does not belong among everything else that does.
793:
Anomie means normlessness — a condition where the shared rules, values, and moral standards that normally hold a society together have broken down, weakened, or become unclear, leaving people without clear guidance for how to live, what to aim for, and how to relate to one another.

To feel the weight of that definition, you need to understand what norms actually do for us. Every society has an invisible rulebook — not just written laws, but unspoken shared understandings: what counts as success, what behavior is acceptable, what people owe each other, what is right and wrong. These norms are the glue of social life. They manage expectations. They give life direction and meaning. They make the world feel predictable and purposeful.

Anomie is what happens when that glue dissolves.
Two Levels: Society and the Individual

Anomie works on two levels, and understanding both is key.

At the societal level, anomie describes a society or community that has lost its normative footing. This happens when old norms collapse faster than new ones can form — during wars, revolutions, economic crashes, or periods of rapid technological or cultural change. Society becomes destabilized. There's no clear, widely shared sense of what the rules are anymore, or whether the rules even apply.

At the individual level, anomie describes the inner experience of living in such a society. A person experiencing anomie feels rootless, disoriented, and purposeless. The sense of "where do I fit?" or "what's the point?" takes over. Life loses its structure and meaning. There is a deep feeling of being disconnected from one's community — like a boat that has lost its anchor and is just drifting.

These two levels feed each other. When society loses its norms, individuals feel lost. When enough individuals feel lost, society's norms erode further.
Durkheim: The Man Who Named It

The concept was developed by the French sociologist Émile Durkheim in the late 1800s, and his thinking is essential to understanding the word properly.

Durkheim had a core belief: human desires are naturally unlimited. Left unchecked, people's appetites — for wealth, status, pleasure, power — are endless. What keeps those desires in check and makes people feel satisfied and grounded is society's norms. Norms tell you what is a reasonable amount to want, what is a realistic and acceptable goal for someone in your position. They regulate desire.

When norms break down, those desires become unregulated. People no longer know what is "enough," what is fair, or what they should expect from life. The result is not freedom — it is misery. Desire without limits is a source of chronic dissatisfaction, not happiness.

Durkheim demonstrated this powerfully in his study of suicide. He found that suicide rates rose not just during economic hardship, but also during times of sudden economic boom. Why? Because both extremes — sudden poverty and sudden wealth — disrupt the normal framework people use to understand their place in the world. When your circumstances change dramatically, the old norms no longer apply and new ones haven't settled in yet. That disorientation — that anomie — makes people vulnerable.

This is one of the most counterintuitive insights the word carries: anomie is not just about suffering from too little. It can arise from too much change in any direction.
Merton: When the Goal Posts Are Reachable Only by Some

American sociologist Robert Merton later extended the concept in a different, equally important direction.

Merton argued that anomie arises when a society promises its members certain goals — say, wealth, success, and upward mobility — but doesn't give everyone a fair and legitimate path to reach those goals. In other words, the goals are broadly advertised, but the means to achieve them are unevenly distributed.

When people are blocked from achieving culturally approved goals through legitimate means (education, hard work, opportunity), they experience a kind of structural frustration. Some give up entirely. Some abandon the goal but keep following the rules mechanically (going through the motions with no real belief). Some reject both the goals and the rules entirely and seek to change the system. And some find illegitimate shortcuts — crime, for instance — to reach the goal by other means.

All of these are responses to anomie in Merton's sense: the painful disconnect between what a society promises you and what it actually makes available to you.

This gave anomie a sharper political edge — it's not just about rapid change, but about structural unfairness that creates normlessness and despair.

If you're trying to picture anomie from the inside, imagine this:

You've always operated by a certain set of rules — work hard and you'll be rewarded, follow the law and you'll be safe, play by the norms and you'll belong. Then something happens — a war, an economic collapse, a massive cultural shift, immigration to a completely foreign society — and those rules no longer seem to apply. Nobody seems to agree on what the rules even are anymore. The things you were taught to value feel hollow or unreachable. You don't know what you're supposed to want, how you're supposed to behave, or where you belong. There's a kind of moral and social vertigo.

That feeling — rootless, purposeless, cut adrift from the fabric of shared meaning — is the lived experience of anomie.

Common triggers include:

Rapid social change. When a society transforms faster than its norms can adapt — through industrialization, revolution, war, or technology — anomie tends to follow. The old rules have stopped working, but the new ones aren't established yet.

Economic instability. Sudden crashes or booms destabilize the expectations people have built their lives around.

Immigration and cultural dislocation. Someone who moves to a new society may find that the norms they internalized no longer apply, and the new norms feel alien. The result can be profound disorientation.

Inequality and broken promises. When a society holds out goals that are structurally inaccessible to large portions of the population (Merton's version), anomie sets in.

Loss of community or institutions. When the churches, neighborhoods, civic groups, or other social structures that carried shared norms weaken or disappear, they take those norms with them.
What Anomie Is NOT (Clearing Up Common Confusion)

Anomie ≠ Anarchy. Anarchy is specifically about the absence of political government or authority. Anomie is about the absence of social and moral norms. A society could have a strong government and still experience deep anomie if its shared values have collapsed.

Anomie ≠ Chaos. Chaos simply means disorder in a general sense. Anomie is a more specific and precise idea — it's the breakdown of the normative framework (the values and rules) that holds social life together. A chaotic scene at a stadium is not anomie. A society where people no longer share any meaningful sense of right, wrong, or purpose is.

Anomie ≠ Alienation. Alienation (especially in the Marxist sense) refers to a feeling of estrangement from one's work, one's fellow human beings, or oneself — often caused by the dehumanizing nature of labor under capitalism. Anomie specifically focuses on the absence or breakdown of norms and standards. The two concepts overlap and can coexist, but they're not the same thing.
How the Word Is Used Today

In academic writing, anomie is still used precisely in the Durkheim and Merton senses — in sociology, criminology, and political science — to analyze crime rates, social unrest, inequality, and suicide.

In more general intellectual conversation, the word is used somewhat more loosely to describe: a pervasive sense of purposelessness in modern life, the moral disorientation of societies undergoing rapid technological change (e.g., the internet and social media dismantling old norms around community, truth, and privacy), or the experience of groups who feel excluded from mainstream society's rules and rewards.

In either case, the word always carries the same essential meaning: the collapse of the shared norms and values that give human life direction, meaning, and social cohesion — and the disorientation, disconnection, and suffering that follow from it.

If you ever need to reach for the word in a sentence, anomie means: a state — in a society or within an individual — in which the shared moral and social norms that give life structure and meaning have broken down, leaving people feeling rootless, purposeless, and cut off from any guiding framework for how to live.
794:
"Anon" means soon, shortly, or in a little while. It tells you that something is going to happen — but not at this exact moment. A small delay is expected, and then the thing will occur.

"She stepped out but will return anon."
(She stepped out but will be back shortly.)

It can also mean "immediately" or "at once." This is the older, stronger sense of the word. When a servant in a classic play shouts "Anon! Anon!" in response to being called, he means "Coming! Coming!" — right away, no delay at all. So the word carries a range: at one end, right this instant; at the other, very soon. Context tells you which sense is meant.

"Fear not — help shall arrive anon."
(Don't worry — help will come soon.)

"Anon, sir, anon!"
(Right away, sir! I'm coming!)

The phrase "ever and anon" is a fixed expression worth knowing. It means now and then, occasionally, or from time to time — something that happens repeatedly but at irregular intervals.

"He would ever and anon glance nervously toward the door."
(Every now and then, he would glance nervously toward the door.)

This is a different flavour from the usual meaning: instead of pointing to one upcoming moment, it describes a pattern of repeated moments spread across time.

Where you'll actually encounter this word: "Anon" is archaic — it belongs to an older era of the English language and is rarely used in natural conversation today. You'll meet it in:

  • Shakespeare's plays (very frequently)
  • The King James Bible
  • Classic poetry and medieval literature
  • Historical fiction that deliberately recreates old-fashioned speech

In modern writing, an author might use "anon" to give a sentence an antique, poetic, or slightly formal feel. If someone says it in everyday speech today, it will sound intentionally old-fashioned — charming to some, odd to others.

One thing to be careful about: In internet culture, "anon" is used as a shortened form of anonymous (as in, someone posting without a name). That is an entirely different usage — a noun, not an adverb — and has nothing to do with what we've discussed here. Don't let it cause confusion.

In a single sentence: As an adverb, anon means "soon" or "immediately" — it signals that something will happen shortly — and in the fixed phrase ever and anon, it means "now and then."
795: Anonymity is the state of being unknown or unidentifiable. When someone has anonymity, their true identity — who they actually are — is hidden from others.

Think of it this way: your identity is like a label attached to everything you do. When you speak, write, or act with your identity attached, people know you did it. Anonymity is when that label is removed — so the action exists, but no one can trace it back to you.

The word comes from the idea of having "no name." An anonymous person, in effect, has no name as far as the people around them are concerned.
What Anonymity Actually Means in Practice

Anonymity doesn't just mean hiding your name. It means hiding any information that could be used to identify you — your face, your location, your voice, your online account, your fingerprints, and so on.

For example:

  • A donation made anonymously means the receiver doesn't know who gave the money.
  • An anonymous tip to the police means the caller's identity is unknown to investigators.
  • Posting online under a fake username can give you anonymity (though not always perfectly — more on that below).
  • Voting in a secret ballot is a form of anonymity — others can't see which candidate you voted for.

Anonymity exists on a spectrum. It's rarely absolute.

  • Full anonymity means no one at all can identify you — not even the platform you're using, not even the government. This is extremely hard to achieve in the modern world.
  • Partial anonymity means some parties know who you are, but others don't. For example, when you call a helpline anonymously, the counselor may not know your name — but your phone company still has a record of the call.
  • Practical anonymity means that while someone could theoretically find out who you are, it's very difficult, unlikely, or too costly for most people to bother — so you function as anonymous for everyday purposes.
Anonymity vs. Related Words You Should Know

These words are often confused with anonymity, so understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of the concept:

Anonymity vs. Confidentiality
Confidentiality means that someone knows your identity but promises to keep it secret. Anonymity means your identity was never revealed to begin with. A doctor keeping your medical records private is confidentiality. Dropping a note in a suggestion box with no name on it is anonymity.

Anonymity vs. Pseudonymity
A pseudonym is a fake name — like a pen name an author uses. Pseudonymity means you're known by a false identity, not by no identity. An author who writes under the name "George Orwell" (whose real name was Eric Blair) had a pseudonym, not anonymity — people knew "George Orwell" as a consistent person; they just didn't know who he really was. Anonymity, strictly speaking, means no consistent identity is attached to you at all.

Anonymity vs. Privacy
Privacy is a broader concept — it means keeping certain information about yourself away from others. Anonymity is one tool for achieving privacy, but they're not the same thing. You can have privacy without anonymity (your name is known, but your medical history is not). You can also have anonymity without full privacy (people don't know who you are, but they can still observe your behavior).

Anonymity serves many important purposes:

1. Protection from retaliation
A whistleblower who exposes corporate corruption, or a witness who reports a crime, may need anonymity to avoid being harmed or punished by powerful people.

2. Freedom of expression
People are often more honest when they know they won't be judged or punished. Anonymous feedback, anonymous surveys, and anonymous reviews tend to be more candid. This is why suggestion boxes and anonymous polls exist.

3. Safety
Victims of abuse, activists living under oppressive governments, or people with controversial political views may rely on anonymity for their physical safety.

4. Fairness
Blind auditions for orchestras — where judges hear musicians play behind a screen — use anonymity to remove bias based on gender or appearance. Similarly, some hiring processes anonymize résumés to reduce racial or gender discrimination.

5. Personal dignity and freedom
The ability to observe the world, participate in conversations, or explore ideas without being constantly watched and recorded is considered by many to be a basic human need.

Anonymity is not purely positive. Because it removes accountability, it can also enable harmful behavior:

  • People may say cruel or hateful things online precisely because they're anonymous and face no consequences.
  • Criminals can exploit anonymity to commit fraud, harassment, or worse.
  • Misinformation spreads more easily when there's no name attached to hold accountable.

This is why anonymity is often a point of tension in society — between the need to protect individuals and the need to hold people accountable for their actions.

In the digital age, true anonymity is surprisingly difficult. Even when you don't use your real name online, you leave behind digital traces — your IP address, the device you're using, patterns in how you type or write, metadata attached to files, and so on. Governments, corporations, and skilled hackers can often "de-anonymize" people even when they believe they're hidden.

This is why privacy researchers and security experts say anonymity is always a matter of degree, not a binary yes/no state.

Anonymity is the condition of being unknown or unidentifiable. It means that your actions, words, or presence cannot be connected back to you as a specific individual. It protects people from judgment, retaliation, and surveillance, but it can also reduce accountability. In the modern world, perfect anonymity is rare — most anonymity is partial, depending on who is trying to identify you and how much effort they're willing to put in.
796:
When something or someone is described as anonymous, it means their identity — most importantly, their name — is either unknown or not revealed to others.

Think of it this way: normally, when you do something, people know it was you who did it. Your name is attached to your action. But when you are anonymous, that connection between you and your action is broken. Nobody knows — or nobody is told — that you were the one behind it.
The Two Real Situations Where "Anonymous" Applies

This is the most important thing to understand: "anonymous" covers two distinct real-world situations.

1. Identity is genuinely unknown — nobody knows who it is.

Sometimes, we simply don't have information about who a person was or is. An old painting might be credited to an "anonymous artist" — meaning nobody knows who painted it. The artist's name has been lost to history. It's not that the artist was hiding; we just don't have that information anymore.

2. Identity is deliberately hidden — someone chooses not to be known.

Other times, a person actively decides to keep their name concealed. Someone might make an "anonymous donation" to a charity — they gave the money, but they don't want anyone to know it was them. Or someone leaves an "anonymous tip" to the police, providing information without saying who they are.

In both situations, the result is identical — you don't know who the person is — but the reason is different. English uses the same word, "anonymous," for both.
Anonymous Can Describe the Person or the Thing They Did

Here's something learners often miss: "anonymous" can be applied either to the person themselves, or to the thing they made or did — and both are perfectly correct.

  • Describing the person: "The donor remained anonymous." → The donor's identity is hidden.
  • Describing the thing: "We received an anonymous letter." → The letter has no name attached to it.

Both of these sentences are about the same concept — hidden identity — just viewed from different angles.
The Extended Meaning: Lacking Any Distinctive Character

"Anonymous" also carries a second meaning, beyond names and identity. It can describe a place, object, or environment that is so plain, bland, and unremarkable that it has no memorable or distinctive character — nothing that makes it stand out or feel unique.

For example: "They spent the night in an anonymous hotel room." This doesn't mean nobody knows who owns the hotel. It means the room was completely forgettable — no personality, no character, nothing special about it at all. It could be any room, anywhere, belonging to no particular place in your memory.

This meaning flows naturally from the core idea. Just as an anonymous person has no name you can attach to them, an anonymous place has no character you can attach to it. Both are, in a sense, faceless.

These are the most frequently used combinations with "anonymous" in everyday English:

  • Anonymous donor / benefactor — someone who gives money or help without revealing their name.
  • Anonymous tip — information passed to authorities or journalists by someone who doesn't identify themselves.
  • Anonymous source — in journalism, a person who gives information but asks not to be named in the published article.
  • Anonymous letter / note — a written message with no name signed to it.
  • Anonymous survey / feedback — a questionnaire where respondents don't give their names, allowing them to answer more freely and honestly.
  • Remain anonymous — to successfully keep one's identity hidden, often over a period of time.
  • Anonymous author / artist — a creator whose true identity is not known.
A Distinction You Must Know: Anonymous vs. Pseudonymous

This is a nuance that even advanced learners sometimes confuse.

Anonymous means no name is given at all — the person is completely unnamed.

Pseudonymous means a false name or pen name is used instead of the real one.

For example: if an author publishes a book with no author name on the cover, they are anonymous. But if they publish under the invented name "A. Writer" (which is not their real name), they are pseudonymous — they have an identity, just a fake one.

Both involve hiding the true identity, but anonymous means nameless, while pseudonymous means falsely named. The two are meaningfully different, even though people sometimes use "anonymous" loosely to mean both.

The most direct antonym of anonymous is identified or named. Depending on context, you might also use known, credited, or attributed.

"The poem was written by an anonymous author" ↔ "The poem was attributed to Shakespeare."

"Anonymous" is about the absence of a known or revealed identity. It applies to people whose names we don't know, to things produced by people whose names are hidden, and — in its extended sense — to places or objects so featureless that they seem to have no identity worth knowing. Whether the namelessness is accidental (lost to history) or intentional (a choice to stay hidden), the word "anonymous" captures it all.
797: The word anorak has two distinct meanings as a noun. Both are correct and widely used, but in very different contexts. You need to know both to fully understand this word.

An anorak is a waterproof or windproof jacket with a hood attached. Its most recognizable feature is that it is usually a pullover style — meaning you slide it over your head to wear it, instead of zipping or buttoning it up the front like a coat. It is typically thick, warm, and practical rather than stylish. Think of the kind of jacket a hiker, a mountaineer, or someone going out in cold, rainy, or windy weather would wear.

Anoraks are strongly associated with outdoor activities — hiking, skiing, camping, birdwatching, and similar pursuits. They prioritize function over fashion. The jacket often has a large front pocket (sometimes called a kangaroo pocket), drawstrings to tighten the hood, and is made from tough, weather-resistant material.

Example sentences:

  • "She pulled on her anorak before heading out into the rain."
  • "He always wore his old green anorak on camping trips."
Meaning 2: A Socially Awkward Enthusiast (British Slang)

This is where the word gets interesting. In British English, "anorak" is also used as a slang term to describe a person who has an obsessive, intense, and very detailed interest in a subject that most people find boring or overly technical.

The key qualities of an "anorak" in this sense are:

  • They know an extraordinary amount about their chosen topic — far more than anyone would normally consider necessary.
  • Their interest is often seen as nerdy, dry, or unfashionable by others.
  • They tend to be socially awkward or at least perceived that way.
  • They may talk about their interest endlessly, even when others aren't interested.

Classic examples of "anorak" hobbies or interests include:

  • Train spotting (memorizing train numbers, schedules, and engine types)
  • Amateur radio operation
  • Stamp collecting
  • Bus route memorization
  • Obsessive statistics about a sport
  • Model railway building

The term is usually mildly mocking or teasing, but it is not always deeply insulting. In many cases, it is used affectionately — almost like fondly poking fun at someone for their harmless but overly intense hobby. Among people who share the same obsessive interest, calling each other "anoraks" can even be a term of solidarity.

Example sentences:

  • "He's a complete anorak — he knows the departure times of every bus in the city."
  • "A group of train anoraks gathered on the platform with their notebooks."
  • "She admits she's a bit of an anorak when it comes to 1970s British television."

The slang meaning grew directly from the jacket meaning, and understanding this makes the word much easier to remember.
